title: Exploring the Prototype of “Gheirat” among Iranian Adults from a Psychological Perspective
summary: This pre-registration contains material related to a study that aims at exploring the concept of “gheirat” among Iranian adults from a psychological perspective. Since this is the first project of its kind to investigate the prototype of gheirat, it is mainly an exploratory study. However, based on researchers’ cultural knowledge and experience, as well as 19 extensive interviews that were conducted prior to designing this study, we have a number of a priori hypotheses and research questions which are presented here. This registration contains two documents: (a) The document labeled “Pre-Registration” includes a brief introduction to the concept of gheirat, an overview of the materials, the main research questions, a priori hypotheses and the corresponding analyses, exclusion criteria and sampling plan. title: Social Cognition & Music Study
summary: 05/28/20 Social & Clinical Neuroscience Lab (PI, Benjamin A. Tabak) Southern Methodist University Department of Psychology Preregistration for “Social Cognition and Music Study” This document is a post-hoc registration of data collection methods and procedures for data that have already been collected. These data were collected between 1/18 and 10/19 and will be used for several purposes. Among its primary objectives, this study aimed to examine the association between empathic accuracy (EA) for social stimuli (i.e., targets in a video describing personal experiences; Kern et al., 2013) and EA for music (i.e., audio recordings of composers playing their musical compositions), as well as emotional congruence for social stimuli with emotional congruence for musical stimuli. Participants were randomly assigned to a condition involving cognitive empathy instructions (e.g., how do you think the target is feeling?) or affective empathy instructions (e.g., how does the target make you feel?) and then watched or listened to a set of social video stimuli and a set of music stimuli. Of note, separate preregistration documents will be drafted to outline any specific research questions and analytical plans using the data collected from this study; these preregistration documents can be found on the principal investigator’s Open Science webpage (OSF link: https://osf.io/r5a4q/). A replication study based on this initial study has previously been pre-registered (https://osf.io/3wqme). Participants: Data collection for this study was conducted in a sample of undergraduate students at Southern Methodist University (SMU) in Dallas, Texas. Following the removal of duplicate cases, a total of 729 participants completed Part 1 of this two-part study, and 452 participants completed Part 2. Participants had to be at least 18 years old to participate and provided informed consent. Procedure: The study took place over two separate sessions (one online and one in-person). In Part 1, participants completed the online measures described below (i.e., questionnaires and behavioral measures) via Qualtrics (Provo, UT). For Part 2, participants were invited into the laboratory for a 1.5-hour in-person session. Upon arrival, participants were randomly assigned to either the cognitive or affective condition of each of the EA tasks (i.e., for both the social EA and music EA tasks). A detailed description of each condition and each task can be found in the Measures section below. Participants completed a first set of questionnaires, as listed in the “Pre-Task Measures” sections below, followed by both the social and music EA tasks. For a subsample of participants, this was followed by an experimental manipulation intended to increase social anxiety in half of the sample, in which participants, based on random assignment, were led to believe that either: a) their performance was being evaluated by peers via a live webcam video conference (i.e., the “performance” condition) or b) that their performance was being recorded for later evaluation by the research team (i.e., the control condition). In the social anxiety condition, a live-streamed video of each participant (i.e., they could see a real-time video of themselves) was displayed on the computer screen via webcam throughout the rest of the study; in addition, participants were told that screen-sharing was enabled and that a number of peers would be remotely watching them as they completed the study. In the control condition, no video was displayed on the computer screen, and participants were told that their responses were recorded for later evaluation by the research team (after the completion of the study). Last, participants completed another set of online measures, as listed in the “Post-Task Measures” section below. Measures: The following measures were included in the study described in this preregistration. These measures were administered separately, as described in the Procedure section above: an online session (“Part 1”), and an in-person session (“Part 2”), which comprised of a first set of questionnaires (“Pre-Task Measures”), the set of social and music EA tasks, and finally, the second set of measures (Post-Task Measures”). 5 = Neither negative nor positive; 9 = Very positive) Affective condition • Participants randomly assigned to the affective condition were asked to continuously rate how negative or positive (scale from 1 = “Very negative” to 9 = “Very positive) they – the participant – were feeling while listening to the recording. • Following each recording, participants were asked to answer the following questions: - “How much did you like that music?” (9-point scale: 1 = Strongly dislike; 5 = Neutral; 9 = Strongly like) - “Overall, do you relate to this music?” (9-point scale: 1 = Not at all; 5 = No opinion; 9 = Very much) - “Overall, did you feel that your emotional reactions to this piece correspond to what the musician intended to express?” (9-point scale: 1 = Not at all; Participants were then shown a second visual stimulus and were asked to respond (using L/R arrow keys) whether the second target image was brighter/darker/smoother/rougher than the first baseline image. title: The Crowd(s) Within
summary: Research question and hypothesis: The average of two estimates from the same person has been shown to be more accurate than each estimate on its own. Here, we investigate how taking a different perspective when making the second estimate (specifically, the perspective of a friend who often agrees with us, or a friend who often disagrees with us), impacts the benefit of averaging. We expect that the benefit of averaging, calculated by subtracting the mean squared error (MSE) of the average of two estimates, from the MSE of the first estimate, will depend on the conditions (i.e., the type of instructions people get on how to make the second estimate), and on the type of question that is asked. Specifically, for questions where the true answer is in the range from 0% to 9% or 91% to 100% (the extreme range questions - see below at the ‘dependent variables’ section), we expect that averaging the first and second estimate, which was made from the perspective of a friend people often disagree with, lowers the accuracy of the average estimate (as compared to the first estimate). This decrease in accuracy of the average estimate is predicted to be larger as compared to the condition in which people are instructed to make a second guess themselves (i.e., same as Vul & Pashler, 2008), or the condition where the second estimate is made from the perspective of a friend people often agree with. For all other questions (the middle range questions - see below at the ‘dependent variables’ section), we expect the reverse. That is, we expect that averaging the first and second estimate, which was made from the perspective of a friend people often disagree with, increases the accuracy of the average estimate (as compared to the first estimate). This increase in accuracy of the average estimate is predicted to be larger as compared to the condition in which the second estimate is a second guess people made themselves (i.e., same as Vul & Pashler, 2008), or the condition where the second estimate is made from the perspective of a friend people often agree with. Design: The study will have a 3 (Perspective taken in the second estimate: Self vs. Agreeing Friend vs. Disagreeing Friend) x 2 (Question Answers: Middle Range vs. Extreme range) mixed subject design. Perspective will be a between-, while Question Answers will be a within-subject factor. In all three between-subject conditions, participants will be instructed to try and answer 12 questions whose answer is always some percentage, ranging from 0% to 100%. Half of the questions will have answers that are in the extreme range. The other half will have answers that are in the middle range. The instructions about the second estimate will depend on the condition (see below). In all three conditions, participants will not be told at the beginning that they will have to make a second estimate. Manipulations: In the self perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be told to make a second guess. The same instructions will be used as in Vul and Pasher (2008) and Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, and Vanpaemel (2014). Specifically, the instruction will be: “We will now ask you to provide a second guess at the answer to each of the twelve questions you were asked in the first session. These answers should not be the same as your previous answers: these should reflect your ‘second guess’.” In the agreeing friend perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be instructed to: “Now picture a friend whose views and opinions are very similar to yours. To illustrate, when discussing politics, you often find yourself agreeing on various issues. How would he or she answer these eight questions? Please answer these questions again, but now as this friend.” In the disagreeing friend perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be instructed to: “Now picture a friend whose views and opinions are very different from yours. To illustrate, when discussing politics, you often find yourself disagreeing on various issues. How would he or she answer these eight questions? Please answer these questions again, but now as this friend.” Dependent variable(s): Participants will be asked to estimate the correct answer of 12 questions whose answer is always a percentage. They will be able to indicate their answer using a slider that ranges from 0% to 100%. As the middle range, we will consider the following questions: 1. What percent of the world’s airports are in the United States? (answer: 32.3%) 2. What percent of the world’s population lives in China, India, and the European Union? (answer: 43.2%) 3. What percent of the world’s countries have a higher fertility rate than the United States? (answer: 57.7%) 4. What percent of the world’s telephone lines are in China, USA, and the European Union? (answer: 53.3%) 5. Saudi Arabia consumes what percentage of the oil it produces? (answer: 32.5%) 6. What percentage of the world’s countries have a higher life expectancy than the United States? (answer: 19.6%) As the extreme range, we will consider the following questions: 1. The area of the USA is what percent of the area of the Pacific Ocean? (answer: 6.3%) 2. What percent of the world’s roads are in India? (answer: 7.3%) 3. What percent of China’s population identifies as Christian? (answer: 5.1%) 4. What percent of the US population is younger than 80? (answer: 96%) 5. What percent of the United Kingdom are internet users? (answer: 94.8%) 6. What percent of the US population owns a cellphone? (answer: 95%) Participants’ responses will be converted to mean squared errors. Data collection procedure: Data will be collected using the mTurk platform. Participants will be paid a fixed amount for their participation which will be limited to individuals from the United States? Analyses: In order to calculate the benefit of averaging, we will subtract the MSE of the average of two estimates from the MSE of the first estimate (rendering a difference score). The higher this number, the higher the benefit of averaging the first- and second estimate (as compared to the accuracy of the first estimate). To test within each respective condition whether the average of the two estimates is more or less accurate than the first estimate (i.e., the within crowd effect), we will use dependent samples t-tests (two-sided). In order to compare the benefit of averaging between the different perspective conditions (i.e., comparing whether the difference score of the MSE of the average and the MSE of the first estimate is different per condition), we will use independent samples t-tests (two-sided). Outliers and exclusions: We will exclude participants that fail an attention check presented at the end of the study. For the attention check, participants have to read the full instructions of the question and check a specific option. We will also exclude participants that report “yes” to having looked up an answer to any question. Sample size: As our main hypothesis concerns comparing the difference scores of the MSE of the average and the MSE of the first estimate across conditions, we will aim to recruit 290 participants per between-subject condition. The sample size was determined by performing a power analysis in G*Power to detect an effect of Cohen’s d = .30, with 95% power, and an alpha of .05. This means we plan to collect 900 participants in total to counteract a potential 2% exclusion rate. We use an effect size of .30 as a previous study we conducted obtained this as the lowest effect size when comparing the benefit of averaging between conditions. We opted to highly power our study to detect this effect, all the while having 80% power or more to detect an effect as low as Cohen’s d = .24. Stopping rule: We will stop data collection once 900 participants in total have taken the study on mTurk. Deviations from the planned number of participants are entirely due to the mTurk platform and are outside of our control. Exploratory measures: We do not include any other measures in our study.

title: Longitudinal associations between prosocial skills and behavioral problems across childhood
summary: A narrative summary of the project follows below. See the attached word-document for the full preregistration (adjusted from the Social Psychology preregistration of Van 't Veer & Giner-Sorolla, 2016). ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ A broad range of studies has shown that prosocial skills and behavioral problems are related constructs. Between persons, children and adolescents higher in prosocial skills are usually lower in behavioral problems such as externalizing and internalizing problems (Flynn et al., 2015; Memmott-Elison et al., 2020). These studies indicate that prosocial skills might be a protective factor for developing behavioral problems and therefore several researchers have suggested that prosocial skills might be an interesting target in interventions for behavioral problems. However, little research has been done on within-person changes of prosocial skills and behavioral problems over time. Put otherwise, do changes within a person in one construct affect performance on the other construct? This is a crucial question with respect to intervention planning. To our knowledge, studies investigating this question so far mainly focused on within-person changes during adolescence (Padilla-Walker et al., 2015; Padilla-Walker et al., 2018). For instance, Padilla-Walker et al. (2018) showed that prosocial behavior and aggression were negatively associated bi-directionally over time. However, since prosocial behavior is a relatively stable trait once developed (Nantel-Vivier et al., 2009; Flynn et al., 2015), it might be important to investigate within-person changes in an earlier phase, during childhood. Moreover, until now it remains unclear whether there are sensitive windows for within-person changes. It is often suggested that early intervention (i.e., during early childhood) results in the largest effect. However, one might suggest that middle childhood is a more suitable period for such within-person changes, as this is a developmental phase where the first friendships emerge and prosocial skills become specifically important (Del Giudice et al., 2009; van der Meulen et al., 2018). To shed light on these important questions, the current project proposes to use random-intercept cross lagged panel models (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al. (2015) to investigate within person effects of prosocial skills on behavioral problems (either internalizing or externalizing) and vice versa during childhood, see Figure 1. To obtain robust results, three indicators of prosocial skills will be used: parental report of prosocial skills (SDQ); parental report of empathy (My Child); and costly donating behavior. Within time points we will test how these prosocial skills relate to both internalizing (SDQ subscales emotional problems + peer problems) and externalizing (SDQ subscale conduct problems + hyperactivity) problem behavior. The evidence on the relation between behavior problems and the three measures of prosocial skills will be aggregated by means of Bayesian evidence synthesis (Kuiper et al., 2013; Zondervan et al., 2019). This encompasses that we will use a set of competing informative hypotheses (Hoijtink, 2012), and evaluate which hypothesis receives most support by the data.

The higher this number, the higher the benefit of averaging the first and second estimate (as compared to the accuracy of the first estimate). We will compare this score among all three conditions. We will also compute a difference score from the first estimate and the extreme estimate, as well as from the second estimate and the extreme estimate. We will compare these scores among all three conditions. For all the tests, we will use mixed-effect models with participants and questions treated as random factors. Outliers and exclusions: We will exclude participants that fail an attention check presented at the end of the study. Participants will have to read the full instructions of the attention question and check a specific option. We will also exclude participants that report “yes” to having looked up an answer to any of the questions. Sample size: As our main hypothesis concerns comparing the difference scores of the MSE of the average and the MSE of the first estimate across conditions, we will aim to recruit 450 participants per between-subject condition. The sample size will enable us to detect a small effect of Cohen’s d = .20 with 85% power, and a Cohen’s d = .30 with > 99% power, as calculated by G*Power. To counteract exclusions and attention check failures, we will increase the total number of participants to 500 per between-subject condition. Stopping rule: We will stop data collection once 1500 participants in total have taken the study on mTurk. Deviations from the planned number of participants are entirely due to the mTurk platform and are outside of our control. Exploratory measures: We do not include any other measures in our study.

title: Childhood Obesity and Stigma toward Parents
summary: In this study, we ask: (1) Do social perceivers stigmatize parents of children with obesity more than parents of average-weight children? (We expect this.) (2) Does stigma transfer from obese children to average-weight parents (as a stigma-by-association account might predict)? (We do not expect this.) (3) Does parent gender moderate stigma toward parents of obese children (such that mothers are more stigmatized), and might this be driven by perceptions that mothers (vs. fathers) are relatively more responsible for offspring appearance/weight? (We explore this.) To explore these questions, Ps are randomly assigned to view one of four stimuli of a mother or father with her/his obese or average-weight daughter. We then ask for feelings toward and inferences about the target parent. To assess stigma in general, we use liking, disliking, and a feeling thermometer. To assess stigma as a parent, we ask about the target being, e.g., a good parent, and we also assess inferences about the target as a parent (e.g., overindulgent To assess a stigma-by-association account, we ask about inferences that the target parent herself/himself, though average-weight, is deemed to have characteristics associated with obesity (e.g., lacks willpower). To assess expectations of parental responsibility for offspring weight, we use one series of items adapted from Sikorski and colleagues (2012) work that parses responsibility for weight---here using parent responsibility, child's own responsibility, societal and cultural factors, genetic factors---and a second items that asks participants to allocate a budget of 100 points to the causal thrust of these four factors for Emma's appearance/weight. We will remove participants who, e.g., fail the CAPTCHA, attention check questions from analyses. We aim to recruit 250 US MTurk Prime participants so that we have usable data for at least 199 participants in analyses, according to power analyses.

title: The Crowd(s) Within
summary: Research question and hypothesis: The average of two estimates from the same person has been shown to be more accurate than each estimate on its own - the within crowd effect. Here, we investigate how taking a different perspective when making the second estimate (specifically, the perspective of a friend we often disagree with), impacts the benefit of averaging. We expect that the benefit of averaging, calculated by subtracting the mean squared error (MSE) of the average of two estimates, from the MSE of the first estimate, will depend on the type of instructions people get on how to make the second estimate. We expect that averaging the first estimate and a second estimate, which was made from the perspective of a friend one often disagrees with, increases the accuracy of the average estimate (as compared to the first estimate). This increase in accuracy of the average estimate is predicted to be larger compared to the condition in which people are only instructed to make a second guess in their second estimate (i.e., same as Vul & Pashler, 2008). Design: The study will have 2 conditions dependent on the perspective taken in the second estimate: Self vs. Disagreeing Friend. In both conditions, participants will be instructed to try and answer 10 questions where they will be asked to estimate the weight of various living and nonliving objects. The instructions for the second estimate will depend on the condition (see below). In both conditions, participants will not be told at the beginning that they will have to make a second estimate. Manipulations: In the self perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be told to make a second guess. The same instructions will be used as in Vul and Pasher (2008) and Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, and Vanpaemel (2014). Specifically, the instruction will be: “We will now ask you to provide a second guess at the answer to each of the ten questions you were asked in the first session. These answers should not be the same as your previous answers: these should reflect your ‘second guess’.” In the disagreeing friend perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be instructed to: “Now picture a friend whose views and opinions are very different from yours. To illustrate, when discussing politics, you often find yourself disagreeing on various issues. How would he or she answer these ten questions? Please answer these ten questions again, but now as this friend.” Dependent variable(s): Participants will be asked to estimate the correct weight of 10 living and nonliving objects in pounds (lb.). Each object will be represented by a picture. They will be able to indicate their answer using a slider. The slider will not have any visible labels and it will start from 0. We will ask the following questions: What is the weight of sumo wrestler Konishiki Yasokichi (in lb.)? (answer: 633 lb) What is the weight of rodeo bull Bodacious (in lb.)? (answer: 1.900 lb) What is the weight of a modern mini cooper (in lb.)? (answer: 2.625 lb) What is the weight of an adult male polar bear (in lb.)? (answer: 1.157,5 lb) What is the weight of a Steinway & Sons concert grand piano (in lb.)? (answer: 990 lb) What is the weight of a Honda Gold Wing motorcycle (in lb.)? (answer: 787 lb) What is the weight of the Liberty Bell (in lb.)? (answer: 2.080 lb) What is the weight of the pole used in caber toss competitions (in lb.)? (answer: 175 lb) What is the weight of a washing machine (in lb.)? (answer: 175 lb) What is the weight of a newborn African elephant (in lb.)? (answer: 234 lb) In order to calculate the benefit of averaging, we will subtract the MSE of the average of two estimates from the MSE of the first estimate (rendering a difference score). The higher this number, the higher the benefit of averaging the first and second estimate (as compared to the accuracy of the first estimate). Data collection procedure: Data will be collected using the mTurk platform. Participants will be paid a fixed amount for their participation which will be limited to individuals from the United States? Analyses: To test within each respective condition whether the average of the two estimates is more or less accurate than the first estimate (i.e., the within crowd effect), we will use dependent samples t-tests (two-sided). In order to compare the benefit of averaging between the different perspective conditions (i.e., comparing whether the difference score of the MSE of the average and the MSE of the first estimate is different per condition), we will use independent samples t-tests (two-sided). Outliers and exclusions: We will exclude participants that fail an attention check presented at the end of the study. For the attention check, participants have to read the full instructions of the question and check a specific option. We will also exclude participants that report “yes” to having looked up an answer to any question. Sample size: We will aim to recruit 450 participants per between-subject condition. The sample size will enable us to detect a small effect of Cohen’s d = .20 with 85% power, and a Cohen’s d = .03 with 99% power as calculated by G*Power. This means we plan to collect 900 participants in total. Stopping rule: We will stop data collection once 900 participants in total have taken the study on mTurk. Deviations from the planned number of participants are entirely due to the mTurk platform and are outside of our control. Exploratory measures: We do not include any other measures in our study.

title: Relations between self-regulation, delinquency and psychopathology from adolescence to adulthood
summary: Data have been made available to the researchers, the following things have been done since: - Files have been compiled - Scores have been calculated for each measure Self-regulation: cognitive, emotional and behavioral Deviance: parent, teacher, self Psychopathology: mood, anxiety and eating disorder symptom count - Missing data were inspected, as a reasonably large amount of participants had missing data at one or more time points it was necessary to look at this more closely. - Data was inspected visually using the ExPanD function from R’s ExPanDaR package for exploring panel data - ICC’s were calculated for the different scales over time - Correlations were inspected for the deviance measures with overlapping timepoints - As the ICC for the teacher measures was low (ICC2 = .27) and correlations with parents at time 2 (r = .34) and with youth at time 3 (r = .19) were lower than for example correlations between parent at time 2 and youth at time 3 (r = .42), the decision was made to not use the teacher reports and only use parent and youth self-report for the deviance measure. Teachers’ scores may have been less reliable due to the limited possibility for students to exhibit these types of antisocial behaviors during class, as well as the limited time teachers spend with students in class (at time 3 students were in secondary school and might have had little time with a single teacher). - For further updates, see sections marked UPDATE below. 1. Research questions 1) Does self-regulation remain stable from early adolescence to adulthood? 2) To what extent can self-regulation causally predict deviance throughout adolescence and adulthood? 3) To what extent can self-regulation longitudinally predict psychopathology? 4) To what extent are there reciprocal relations between self-regulation and deviance/psychopathology over time? 2. Hypotheses 1) There is medium to high stability of self-regulation over time. There is less stability of self-regulation in vulnerable groups. 2) Low self-regulation predicts deviance over adolescence and adulthood. 3) Low self-regulation predicts psychopathology over adolescence and adulthood. 4) There are reciprocal relations between low self-regulation and deviance/psychopathology over time (i.e., low self-regulation predicts deviance/psychopathology which in turn predicts low self-regulation at the next time point). 3. Data The current study will make use of existing data from a large longitudinal study conducted by CEDAR. The data was not accessible by the researchers at time of registration, coding books were available and one researcher had previously used other parts of this dataset. Researchers looked into the official criminal records in order to assess if these were useful as a measure, but did not conduct any analyses on this data. The sample consists of a group of over 900 participants that were followed from age 10-12 to age 30, during eight measurements. The precise number of participants in the group, and the amount of dropout is presently unknown, making it difficult to specify exact models for analysis. UPDATE: Data for one or more of the measures at one or more time points is available for 772 individuals. Variables of interest 1) Self-regulation A 92-item dysregulation inventory Mezzich, Tarter, Giancola, & Kirisci (2001) will be used to measure cognitive, emotional and behavioral self-regulation. This data was present at all 8 measurement points. 2) Deviance Deviance will be measured using overlapping items from the CBCL parent/teacher reports (before age 16) and the Youth/Adult self-report (after age 16). Items differ slightly across different measures, but concern the same content. Items seem to reflect major and minor deviance at face value. As double measure (i.e., parent/teacher, teacher/youth) were taken at certain time points, it will be checked if both tap in to the same underlying construct. A confirmatory factor analysis will be done to ensure all items load on a single deviance factor. The items and alternative wordings can be found below. Major deviance items | alternative wordings Destroys property belonging to (his/her family or) others | I (damage or) destroy things belonging to others Gets in many fights | I get in many fights Physically attacks people | I physically attack people Steals | I steal Threatens people | I threaten to hurt people Minor deviance items | alternative wordings Cruelty, bullying or meanness to others | I am mean to others Destroys his/her owns things | I (damage or) destroy my (own) things Doesn’t seem to feel guilty after misbehaving | I don't feel guilty after doing something I shouldn’t Hangs around with other who get in trouble | I hang around with kids/others/people who get in trouble Lying or cheating | I lie or cheat Temper tantrums or hot temper | I have a hot temper Used alcohol or drugs for non-medical purposes | I use alcohol or drugs for non-medical purposes; I use drugs (other than alcohol (and nicotine)) for non-medical purposes Criminal records Criminal records were consulted around 19 years of age, and will be taken in as part of the deviance measure, or as a separate construct, depending on how well these items converge. UPDATE: criminal records where not obtained and will not be used in the model. 3) Psychopathology Psychopathology was measured in a variety of ways at different time points within the data collected by CEDAR. For the current study the aim was to find a general measure of mental health functioning, rather than looking at specific mental disorder diagnoses. There are two measures in the data which might make this possible. First is the Global Assessment of Functioning scores, given by clinicians during diagnostic interviews using the Psychiatric History Marker. Second is the use of symptom counts of the SCID. Both methods have limits, the first due to the possibility of unreliable GAF scores due to the interviews being done by different clinicians. SCID symptom counts on the other hand might show large variation in severity, and when looking at individuals with similar scores, one might have a clinical disorder, where the other might have a collective of minor symptoms scattered over different disorders. UPDATE: Based on a general glance of the data, the GAF scores did not seem like a good option, as they were given infrequently and with little variation. Therefore it was decided to use the SCID items as an indicator of psychopathology. Items representing symptoms that were scored in a yes/no format were taken as indicators of psychopathology (e.g., “Have you ever been particularly nervous or anxious for an extended period of time?”). Furthermore, items that could indicate the gravity of the disorder were counted if they were in a yes/no format (i.e., for social phobia, several situations were listed in which someone could experience fear, e.g., speaking in public, the presence of fear in each of these situations was counted separately, as fear in many situations would indicate more severe psychopathology). UPDATE: The SCID is a diagnostic interview, regarding symptoms of many known mental health conditions. Data was available on Major Depression, Dysthymic Disorder, Manic Syndrome, Psychotic and Associated Symptoms, Anxiety disorders (Panic Disorder, Agoraphobia, Social Phobia, Simple Phobia, Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder), Somatoform Disorders, Eating Disorders (Anorexia and Boulimia Nervosa), Adjustment Disorder, Antisocial Personality Questionnaire Supplement, Conduct Disorder Supplement. For the purpose of the current study, mood, anxiety and eating disorder items will be used, as these are sufficiently distinct from both deviance and self-regulation, but may still influence them. Based on the items present in the questionnaire, it did not seem logical to use somatoform items, as the presence of a potential medical cause is not known. With regard to Antisocial and Conduct items, there seems to be too large of an overlap with the items present in both the deviance and the self-regulation items (i.e., items concerning impulsive and criminal acts) to the point where the items would no longer be informative. With regard to psychotic symptoms, although these symptoms might lead to deviant behavior, or be caused by deviant behavior (i.e., drug use), it is not deemed sufficiently informative to aid the question asked in the current study, also a link with self-regulation is not expected. Adjustment disorder was not taken along as the items are not symptoms on their own, but refer to how well a person deals with his/her symptoms. Furthermore, combining symptoms of these different disorders is unlikely to provide us with a unidimensional, interpretable scale for psychopathology. What remains are three classes of internalizing disorders, mood, anxiety and eating disorders, that are separate from, but may be related to self-regulation (e.g., a lack of emotion regulation for mood and anxiety disorders, a lack of cognitive or behavioral regulation for eating disorders) and/or deviance (e.g., mood disorders may limit the possibilities for committing deviant acts, anxiety disorders may develop because of deviant behavior). UPDATE: The selected items of the mood, anxiety and eating disorders will be scored as 1 (present) or 0 (not present/not scored). The “not scored” part applies to items that were not scored due to the way the SCID is taken, that is, when a person answers negatively on a specific item they would not be asked questions that would specify the symptoms further (e.g., if someone has never experienced a panic attack, no further questions about panic attacks were asked). As clinicians decided it was not needed to score these items, for the purpose of the current study, they were scored as absent. The symptom count will be averaged for mood, anxiety and eating disorders separately, and then averaged on total. Averaging on disorder level was done to avoid the number of items for a single disorder to affect the total score for a participant, as some disorders had more items assessing smaller aspects of the disorder. 4. Analyses (preliminary) In order to inspect basic stability of self-regulation over time, Spearman’s rank order correlations will be used. Correlation coefficients of the vulnerable and general group will be transformed and compared to each other. A cross-lagged panel design using structural equation modeling will be used to inspect the relations between the different variables over time for the whole group (as the underlying mechanisms should be the same). Two theoretical models will be compared for model fit, one with only effects of self-regulation on crime/psychopathology and one with reciprocal relationships. Changes may be made in an exploratory way in order to improve model fit. UPDATE: The cross-lagged panel design will be tested using a Random Intercept Cross Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) using structural equation modeling. This will be done in R, using the Lavaan package. In the RI-CLPM latent factors are calculated for each construct over measurement points, with the weight of each regression set to 1. This is done to remove between-person effects from the model, so that within-person changes can be observed. Missing data will be estimated using the full information maximum likelihood (FIML) method, which is present in the Lavaan package, when running the SEM model (most likely using a robust version for non-normal data, i.e., MLR). UPDATE: As on first inspection of the variables there was little variance in the psychopathology measure (i.e., most people did not show any signs of psychopathology), it was decided to run and compare a model with only self-regulation and deviance, and a full model including psychopathology. As one model is nested in the other, it will be possible to compare both models statistically. After the best of both models is selected, adjustments might be made in an exploratory way, to improve model fit.

title: Appreciation and Perceived Division of Labor
summary: Study Rationale and Aims The aim of the current study was to assess the roles that (a) feeling appreciative for one’s partner and (b) feeling appreciated by one’s partner play in how people perceive the division of labor (DoL) in their household and associations with satisfaction with DoL and overall relationship satisfaction. More specifically, we are interested in four questions: 1. Does feeling appreciative for one’s partner predict seeing one’s partner as doing a greater share of DoL? 2. Does feeling appreciative for one’s partner moderate the association between one’s own perceptions of DoL and one’s partner’s report of DoL, such that the association between own and partner DoL is stronger (more agreement) for those who feel more (vs less) appreciative of their partner? 3. Does feeling appreciated by a partner moderate the association between perceived DoL and satisfaction with DoL? That is, perceiving that one does a greater share of the DoL could be associated with feeling less satisfied with the DoL, but is this effect attenuated if people feel more (vs less) appreciated by their partners? 4. Does feeling appreciated by one’s partner moderate the relationship between perceived DoL and relationship quality? That is, perceiving that one does a greater share of the DoL could be associated with lower relationship satisfaction, but is this effect attenuated if people feel more (vs less) appreciated by their partners? We explain these predictions and intended analyses in the planned analyses section below. This study is part of a larger study on cohabiting couples coping during the COVID-19 pandemic conducted by the Well-being, Health, and Interpersonal Relationships Lab (WHIRLab) at the University of Michigan and as such, includes many other variables of interest. Sociodemographic information was also collected at background. SEE ATTACHED ANALYSIS PLAN FOR FULL PREREGISTRATION OF ANALYSES.

title: The Pervasive Impact of Ignorance
summary: 1) Have any data been collected for this study already? No, no data have been collected for the study yet. 2) What's the main question being asked or hypothesis being tested in this study? Previous research has shown that a host of different judgments are influenced by norm violations (e.g., acting immorally). We plan to ask whether these effects are moderated by whether or not the agent was ignorant of the relevant norm that was being violated. Below, we quickly describe each previous study, or manipulation and the relevant predictions. Phillips & Knobe, 2009: Previously, this research found that participants rated a ship captain as less forced to throw something overboard if throwing that thing overboard was immoral (e.g., passengers) vs. not immoral (e.g., cargo). Here, we manipulate whether the ship captain is reasonably ignorant of what he is throwing overboard, and thus whether or not the action is immoral. We predict that the difference in force judgments between the ignorant immoral (unaware of passengers) and neutral (cargo) conditions will be smaller than the difference between the informed immoral and neutral conditions, or that there will be no difference. Fraser & Knobe, 2008 Previously, this research found that when administrative assistants are allowed to take pens and professors are not, if both an administrative assistant and a professor take the last two pens, participants agreed that the professor was more of a cause of the problem than the administrative assistant. We manipulate whether the professor is ignorant that she is doing something wrong. We predict that the difference in causal judgements between the ignorant immoral (not knowing they’re not allowed to take pen) and neutral (allowed to take pen) conditions will be smaller than the difference between informed immoral and neutral causal judgements. Cushman, Knobe, & Sinnott Armstrong, 2008 Previously, this research found that participants are more likely to say that a doctor who has stated his dislike of homeless people, ended a homeless man's life (vs. allowed it to end) when the doctor acted immorally (disconnecting the homeless man from a ventilator to avoid wasting time and resources) compared to when the doctor acted neutrally (disconnecting the man from the ventilator to preserve his dignity). In both cases, the man will die in a week or two no matter what the doctor does. We manipulate whether the doctor is ignorant of whether or not the man is homeless. We predict that the difference in the extent to which participants judge the doctor to have ended (vs. allowed to end) the homeless man’s life will be smaller between the ignorant immoral (unaware the man is homeless) and neutral condition than in the informed immoral and neutral conditions. Knobe, 2003: Previously, this research found that participants were much more likely to judge a chairman as bringing about a side-effect of a new program intentionally if that side effect is morally bad (e.g., harming the environment) than when it is morally good (e.g., helping the environment), though the chairman expressed that he only cares about the program’s profits in both conditions. We additionally manipulate whether the chairman and everyone in the company are ignorant to the true environmental impact of the new program. We predict that the difference in judgements of the chairman’s intentionality in bringing about the side effects between the immoral (harming the environment) and neutral (helping the environment) conditions will be weaker when the vice president is ignorant of the harmful environmental impact. Phillips et al., 2015: Previously, this research found that when agents are living a morally bad life (e.g., a nurse poisoning sick children), participants rated those agents as less happy than those acting morally (e.g., a nurse helping sick children) even though the agents mental states were uniformly described as satisfying the criteria for happiness. We manipulate whether the nurse is ignorant that she is doing something wrong. We predict that the difference in judgements of the nurse’s happiness between the immoral (harming children) and neutral (helping children) conditions will be lesser when the nurse is ignorant of the fact that what she is doing is wrong. Young and Phillips, 2011 Previously, this research found that participants more agreed with the active form of the sentence “The captain forced the sailor…” than the passive form of the sentence “The sailor was forced by the captain…” but only when the action the captain pressured the sailor to do was immoral. We manipulate whether the captain and sailor are ignorant of the immorality of the action and we predict that when the captain and sailor are both ignorant, this effect is weaker: that participants will more equally judge that the captain forced the sailor to the action and that the sailor was forced by the captain to do the action (i.e., smaller or no difference in the force judgments). Young and Phillips, 2011 Previously, this research found that participants agree more with the active form of the sentence “The chief forced the doctor...” than the passive form of the sentence “The doctor was forced by the chief...” when the action the chief pressured the doctor to do was immoral (e.g., kill the patient). We manipulate whether the chief and doctor are ignorant of the immorality of the action and predict that the effect of active v. passive forms of sentences on perceived fault is weaker when the chief and doctor are ignorant. Kominsky & Phillips, 2019; Icard, et al., 2017 Previously this research has found (across four different scenarios) that when an agent acts immorally and contributes to an outcome, people judge that agent to be more of a cause of the outcome (and find changes to that agent’s actions to be more counterfactually relevant) than another agent who acted morally but whose action was also necessary for the outcome to occur (e.g., in a conjunctive causal structure). In contrast to this condition in which both actions were necessary, the agent who acted immorally is judged to be less of a cause of the outcome if both agents’ actions are independently sufficient to bring about the outcome (i.e., a disjunctive causal structure). We created new conditions in which the agents are not aware that they are acting immorally, and predict that in these conditions, both effects will weaken: In both the conjunctive and disjunctive causal structures, participants causal judgments will show less of a difference between the two agents. Petitt & Knobe, 2009 Previously, this research found that the impact of moral judgement plays a role in the application of many concepts that involves holding or displaying a positive attitude toward an outcome, specifically intentional action, desire, ‘decided’, and arbitrary expressions of positive attitude (‘advocated’ and ‘in favor of’). Likewise, they find attributions of negative attitudes like opposition are weaker when an outcome is morally bad vs good. We manipulate whether the agent in a vignette is ignorant that they are acting immorally, and predict that when the agent is ignorant, the pervasive effect of moral judgement is weaker: participants will disagree more that the agent was holding or displaying a positive attitude to the negative side effect (and disagree less to the agent holding a negative attitude) when the agent is ignorant of that side-effect than when the agent knows that the chosen action will have that side-effect. Szabo & Knobe, 2003 Previously, this research demonstrated that the effect of norm violations found in previous research on force, intention, causation extended to ‘modal proxies’ of these judgments. For example, just as people would say an agent was more forced to do a morally neutral action than an immoral action, they more agreed with the sentence ‘Given the circumstances, the agent had to do that action’ when the action was morally neutral than when the action was immoral. We ask whether both these effects on the relevant modal proxies are affected by the agent’s knowledge of the norm. Specifically, we predict that when the agent is ignorant that their action will have a negative consequence, agreement with the modal proxies will differ from the case in which the agent knew that the action would have a negative consequence (and be more similar to the cases in which the agents’ actions did not have a negative consequence). Uttich and Lombrozo, 2010 Previously, this research found that participants agreed it was more appropriate to say an agent brought about a side effect intentionally in norm-violating cases than in norm-conforming cases for both moral and conventional norm violations. We manipulate whether the agent is ignorant that they are violating a conventional norm. We predict that the difference in judgement of intentionality between the ignorant norm violating and the neutral condition will be smaller than in the intentional norm violating and neutral conditions. 3) Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they will be measured. We outline each dependent variable for each relevant study below: Phillips & Knobe 2009 Participants will rate their agreement with the following sentence: “The ship captain was forced to cut the cargo loose and let it fall into the sea.” On a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). In all conditions, participants will be also asked to rate their agreement with the following statements: “The captain knew that a number of illegal passengers were hiding in the cargo boxes.” and “The captain should have known whether or not a number of illegal passengers were hiding in the cargo boxes.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). Fraser & Knobe, 2008 Participants will rate their agreement with the following sentence: “Prof. Smith caused the problem.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). Young and Phillips, 2011 In the active conditions, participants will rate their agreement with the following sentence: “The captain forced the sailor to cut the cargo loose and let it fall into the sea.” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). Kominsky & Phillips, 2019; Icard, et al., 2017 Participants will rate their agreement with one of the following sentences: “They were able to start the car because of Billy.” [“Billy caused the bridge to collapse.”] [“Billy caused the motion detector to go off.”] [“Billy caused the emails to be deleted.”] On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). In thinking about who could have acted differently, participants will also rate how relevant or irrelevant it would be to focus on the following: “Billy”. On a scale from 1 (not at all relevant) to 7 (highly relevant). In all conditions, participants will also be asked to rate their agreement with the following statements: “Billy knew that [he was not allowed to take the Bartlett Battery.] [his signal meant that he was supposed to stop.] [he was not supposed to come in at 9am that day.] [he was not supposed to log into the central computer in the mornings.]” and “Billy should have known whether or not [he was not allowed to take the Bartlett Battery.] [his signal meant that he was supposed to stop.] [he was not supposed to come in at 9am that day.] [he was not supposed to log into the central computer in the mornings.]” On a scale from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 7 (Strongly agree). In addition they also rated their agreement with one of the four corresponding statements: “The chairman should have known whether or not the policy would harm the environment.”, “The assistant manager should have known whether or not he was making the employees do more work.”, “The CEO should have known whether or not the policy would harm the environment.”, “The man should have known whether or not he was detonating the bomb.”. All answers were given on a scale from 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree). Szabo & Knobe, 2003 Participants will be asked to rate their agreement (1- disagree, 7-agree) with one of the following sentences or sets of sentences. For the study involving force: “Given the circumstances, the captain had to cut the cargo loose and let it fall into the sea.” For the study involving causation: “Given the actions of the professor, the problem had to occur.” / “Given the actions of the administrative assistant, the problem had to occur.” And for the study with intentional action: “Jake hit the [bulls-eye/his aunt] through sheer luck.” In all conditions, participants will also be asked to rate their agreement with the following statements: “The captain knew a number of illegal passengers were hiding in the cargo boxes.”[“Prof. Smith knew that only administrative assistants are allowed to take pens.”] [“Jake knew that the rifle bullets would pierce through the target and hit his aunt.”] and [“The captain should have known whether or not a number of illegal passengers were hiding in the cargo boxes.”[“Prof. Smith should have known that only administrative assistants are allowed to take pens.”] [“Jake should have known whether or not the rifle bullets would pierce through the target and his aunt.”] Uttich and Lombrozo, 2010 Participants will be asked to answer one of the following questions: “How appropriate is it to say the chairman of the board [the Chief of Medicine] [the boss] intentionally made Gizmos [Scrubs] [Truck Trailers] colored darker than blue?” On a scale from 1 (not at all appropriate) to 7 (very appropriate). In all conditions, participants will also be asked to rate their agreement with the following statements: “The chairman of the board [the Chief of Medicine] [the boss] knew the color conventions of Gizmos [Scrubs] [Truck Trailers].” and “The chairman of the board [the Chief of Medicine] [the boss] should have known the color conventions of Gizmos [Scrubs] [Truck Trailers].” on a scale from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree) 4) How many and which conditions will participants be assigned to? Participants will be randomly assigned to see three conditions in random order (one non-norm violation condition, one knowledgeable norm violation condition, and one ignorant norm violation condition). After the order in which they receive these three conditions is randomly determined, they will be randomly assigned to one of the paradigms employed in previous research (as listed above) for each of the three conditions. We will aim to collect >30 responses for each dependent variable in each study being replicated and extended. In the original studies, there are 27 key comparisons that we will aim to replicate and extend. Thus, we plan to collect 1500 participants, which should give us an average of ~55 responses per dependent variable. 5) Specify exactly which analyses you will conduct to examine the main question/hypothesis. Primary Analysis: First, we will ask, in each individual study, whether we replicated the originally observed effect. In all cases where we are able to replicate the original effect, we will then do the same statistical test, but replace the original knowledgeable norm-violation condition with the new ignorant norm-violation condition. Our hypothesis is that the effect sizes (all converted to r) for the second analysis will be smaller than the for the first analysis. Given this, our statistical approach will be meta-analytic: to statistically investigate whether our hypothesis is correct, we will collect the effect sizes from both our replications of the original statistical tests and the new statistical tests involving the ignorance conditions and analyze them by comparing a series of linear mixed-effects models (implemented in the lme4 package in R). More specifically, we will build a model that predicts effects sizes with a fixed effect for whether the non-norm violation condition was compared to a knowledge norm-violation or an ignorant norm violation (call this fixed effect “epistemicState”). This model will also include random intercepts and slopes for the paradigm that was being replicated and extended (epistemicState | paradigm) and perhaps (epistemicState | participant) -- and then simplify down to just a random intercept for paradigm or participant in case of convergence problems. We will then compare this model to one that does not include the fixed effect “epistemicState” but is otherwise identical (including the random effects structure) using the anova function in R. Secondary analyses: In addition, we will also analyze both knowledge questions that were included as dependent variables. Our key question with these additional dependent variables is whether either or both of them mediate the effect of “epistemicState” hypothesized above. Accordingly, we will calculate the effect size for the difference for both the “knows” and “should know” questions in a manner similar to the primary analysis. We will first conduct the statistical tests from the original paper but now on responses to the “knows” questions, comparing the non-norm violation conditions to the knowledgeable norm violation conditions. Secondly, we will then conduct an identical set of statistical tests but compare the non-norm violation conditions to the ignorant norm violation conditions. This will give us a set of paired effect sizes for the “knows” questions similar to those for the original dependent variables in the primary analysis. The same process will then be used to calculate the effect sizes involving the “should know” questions. Finally, we will conduct a multiple mediation analysis where we enter both the “knows” and “should know” effect sizes as potential mediators of the effect of “epistemicStates” on the effect sizes for the original dependent variables.

title: Preschooler's search for empirical evidence following a surprising claim
summary: Hypotheses: In Ronfard, Chen, & Harris (2017), preschool children may not have sought empirical evidence to test the adult’s surprising claim that the smallest Russian doll was the heaviest because the task was too demanding - children had to compare the dolls across two dimensions (i.e., weight as well as height). Preschool children might gather empirical evidence to test an adult’s surprising claim when presented with a claim that is easier to test. Thus, in this study children will be presented with such a claim – that a rock is soft rather than hard. This claim requires investigation because it refers to an “invisible” property but it does not require the child to compare two objects. It is not a relative claim. It is also a more improbable claim than the one used in the “dolls” paradigm. It may be that younger children are more likely to test a seemingly impossible claim (a soft rock) than an improbable claim (a very heavy small object). In an initial follow-up study (ROCK1), we presented children with five rocks and asked them about whether each rock was hard or soft. Children got confirming testimony that all of the rocks were hard, except for the last one where half of the children were told that the rock was indeed hard and the other half were told that that rock was soft. After testing about 38 children, we stopped data collection. About half of the children had to be discarded based on our prespecified criterion that children had to endorse all five rocks as hard. One reason for this high number of children who had to be discarded is that despite their intuitions that rocks are hard, they were faced with five rocks and asked the same questions multiple times. The pragmatics of the situation may have led them to infer that one of the rocks must be soft given that the experimenter keeps asking the same question. This led us to a redesign of the study where children are introduced to three distinct objects: a rock, a sponge like material, and a hacky sack. We have also added survey measures Early Parenting Attitudes Questionnaire (with measures of parental authoritarianism added) and the Inventory of Children’s Individual Differences. We make the following predictions: (1) Children who are told that one of the rocks is soft (rather than hard) will more often state that one of the rocks they saw is soft. That is, children will endorse the counter-intuitive testimony. (2) If task complexity or the type of claim (relative weight rather than hardness) accounts for preschool children’s failure to test the adult’s claim in prior work then preschool children who are told that a rock is soft (counter-intuitive condition) should display more exploration of the rock relative to the other two objects, as compared with children who are told that a rock is hard (confirming condition). In addition to influencing the amount of exploration that children conduct, the testimony may also influence how quickly children explore the rock, with children in the counterintuitive condition being quicker than children in the confirming condition to touch the rock. (3) Children who were told that one of the rocks is soft will be more likely to mention the rock’s hardness when the experimenter returns to the room than children who were told none of the rocks are soft. (4) Children in the counter-testimony who touched or picked up the rock they were told was soft will be more likely to deny on the final judgement question that any of the rocks are soft than children who did not conduct such exploration. (5) We expect that lower parental authoritarianism will predict greater exploration in the counterintuitive condition only. (6) We expect that individual differences in children’s personality traits will have an influence on how often children explore the objects. We do not have strong predictions and consider these analyses exploratory. Methods: Design: Child Exploration: Children will be randomly assigned to either receive testimony that confirms their belief that rocks are hard or testimony that contradicts this belief – i.e. that a rock is soft. They will complete 5 phases. 1. Initial Judgment. The experimenter (E) will present preschool children with 3 objects (rock, sponge like material, hacky sack). E will ask whether the rock is hard or soft. 2. Testimony. In one condition, children will be told that they are correct– i.e., that the rock is indeed hard. In another condition, children will be told that they are wrong and that the rock is soft rather than hard. 3. Post-testimony Judgment. After receiving testimony from E, children will be asked again whether each rock is hard or soft. 4. Opportunity to Explore. E will exit the room and tell children they can play with the rocks. Thus, children may or may not decide to check the rock when they are left alone. By touching or lifting the rock children can assess whether the rock indicated by the experimenter is actually soft (a false claim). 5. Final Judgment with E1. The experimenter will ask children whether the rock is hard. Parent-child Exploration: The parent child exploration phase will take place after the child exploration phase. This is done so that the parent-child interaction does not prime child exploration in the exploration task. The parent-child exploration activity will be analyzed as part of another study. Parents will be told that we want them to look over the book with their child and that there is no wrong or right way to do it. We will ask them to interact with their child as they naturally would at home. The wordless picture book parents will be given will have 26 pages. Across two pages, a surprising event will be depicted, e.g. image #1 shows a scuba diver, and image #2 shows the scuba diver swimming towards a house that’s underwater. Some of the events were taken from the stimuli developed by Frazier, Wellman, and Gelman (2009), e.g. a nest with a turtle in it. Other Measures: (1) Early Parenting Attitudes Survey + Parental Authoritarianism (2) Inventory of Children’s Individual Differences Planned sample 120 total children. 20 4-year olds in each condition, 20 5-year olds in each condition, and 20 6-year olds in each condition. A sample size of 20 is enough to detect a similar effect size for counter testimony that we have found with older children (prior work had used a sample size of 16). Given prior work (Ronfard, Chen, Harris, 2018) we also expect age-related differences in children’s exploration. Specifically, we expect older children to explore more than the younger children. Exclusion criteria Children’s data will be excluded if children initially identify the rock as soft. Children and their parents will still complete the entire experiment. Children’s data will also be excluded if the child didn’t finish the experiment, e.g. left room halfway due to distress. Analysis plan Coding: (1) Responses Code: children’s verbal responses to E’s question “Is the rock hard or soft?” all three times, i.e. initially, after E’s testimony, and after opportunity to explore objects. Spontaneous comments: Code whether the child spontaneously state that the rock cannot be soft following the initial testimony and also whether the child spontaneously mentions whether the rock is hard after the exploration phase. (2) Exploration First item explored: Record which object is explored first (e.g. touching, picking up, squeezing, pushing down). This will also include latency (in seconds) for first item explored. Latency to explore the rock: Measure in seconds how long until children interact with the rock (touching, picking up, squeezing, pushing down). Amount of time spent interacting with each item: continuous measure of interacting with the items (includes all behaviors) coded separately for each item (three measures). If the child is building a tower with the items, code that the child is interacting with all those items. If the child stops and restarts touching the same object with a break of 2 or less seconds in between, code this as one touch (e.g. poking an object repeatedly). Expressions of surprise: verbal and non-verbal reactions when they interact with the rock (e.g. surprised facial expression). (3) Book: This data will be used for a different study. Analyses: (1) Initial and post-testimony judgments Of children who initially stated that the rock is hard (100%), how many continued to endorse this after hearing E’s testimony? Is there a significant difference between conditions in how many said “soft” when asked after E’s testimony? Does this differ by age? We will conduct a repeated measures logistic regression. We will regress children’s endorsement of rock = hard on condition, age, and the interaction between condition and age. (2a) First object explored Is there a difference between conditions in which object the children are most likely to touch first? Conduct: We will conduct a multinomial logistic regression. We will regress children’s touch of each item on condition, age, and the interaction between condition and age. (2b) Time until rock is touched Is there a difference between conditions in how long it takes for children to touch the rock for the first time? Conduct: 2 X 3 ANOVA on the amount of time it took children to explore the rock (for children who did touch the rock), Condition (2: Confirming; Counter), Age (3: 4-, 5-, 6-years-old). (3) Children’s exploration of the rock (duration) a- The first analysis will focus on looking at the amount of time that children examine each item by condition. Conduct: 3 X 3 X 2 mixed effect ANOVA on the total amount of time spent on each item: within subject factor of Item (3: rock, a sponge like material, and a hacky sack), between subject factors of Age (3: four, five, six) and Condition (2: confirming and counterintuitive). b- The second set of analyses will focus on individual differences. Specifically, we will look at the personality traits and parental authoritarianism. We will look at whether there is a main effect of these variables (influences children in both conditions equally) or whether there is an interaction (whether it influences children more in the counterintuitive condition). (4a) Post-exploration confrontation as a function of condition Is there a difference in probability of children commenting on the rock’s hardness when E returns to the room depending on the condition they’re in? Conduct: Conduct a logistic regression. We will regress whether children spontaneously commented (coded as 1) or not (coded as 0) on condition, age, and the interaction between condition and age. (4b) Post-exploration judgments as a function of exploration Is there a difference in probability of children in the counter-intuitive condition saying “the rock is hard” (final judgment) depending on whether they explored the rock? Conduct: Logistic regression. Only children in counterintuitive condition. Regress whether they state the rock is hard on the last question on whether they interacted with the rock (coded as 1) or not (coded as 0), age, and the interaction between age and using at least one strategy. • We will also examine the role of individual difference measures personality traits and parental authoritarianism.

title: The Crowd(s) Within
summary: Research question and hypothesis: The average of two estimates from the same person has been shown to be more accurate than each estimate on its own. Here, we investigate how taking a different perspective when making the second estimate (specifically, the perspective of a friend who often disagrees with us), impacts the benefit of averaging. We expect that the benefit of averaging, calculated by subtracting the error of the average of two estimates from the error of the first estimate, will depend on the type of instructions people get on how to make the second estimate. We expect that averaging the first and a second estimate made from the perspective of a friend one often disagrees with increases the accuracy of the average estimate (as compared to the first estimate). This increase in accuracy of the average estimate is predicted to be larger compared to the condition in which people are only instructed to make a second guess in their second estimate (i.e., same as Vul & Pashler, 2008). Design: The study will have 2 conditions dependent on the perspective taken in the second estimate: Self vs. Disagreeing Friend. In both conditions, participants will be instructed to try and answer 6 questions whose answer is always some percentage, ranging from 0% to 100%. The instructions for the second estimate will depend on the condition (see below). In both conditions, participants will not be told at the beginning that they will have to make a second estimate. Manipulations: In the self perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be told to make a second guess. The same instructions will be used as in Vul and Pasher (2008) and Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, and Vanpaemel (2014). Specifically, the instruction will be: “We will now ask you to provide a second guess at the answer to each of the six questions you were asked in the first session. These answers should not be the same as your previous answers: these should reflect your ‘second guess’.” In the disagreeing friend perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be instructed to: “Now picture a friend whose views and opinions are very different from yours. To illustrate, when discussing politics, you often find yourself disagreeing on various issues. How would he or she answer these six questions? Please answer these six questions again, but now as this friend.” Dependent variable(s): Participants will be asked to estimate the correct answer of 6 questions whose answer is always a percentage (cf. Vul & Pashler, 2008). They will be able to indicate their answer using a slider that ranges from 0% to 100%. What percent of the world’s airports are in the United States? (answer: 32.3%) What percent of the world’s population lives in China, India, and the European Union? (answer: 43.2%) What percent of the world’s countries have a higher fertility rate than the United States? (answer: 57.7%) What percent of the world’s telephone lines are in China, USA, and the European Union? (answer: 53.3%) Saudi Arabia consumes what percentage of the oil it produces? (answer: 32.5%) What percentage of the world’s countries have a higher life expectancy than the United States? (answer: 19.6%) Participants’ responses will be converted to mean squared errors (MSE). Data collection procedure: Data will be collected using the Prolific platform. Participants will be paid a fixed amount for their participation which will be limited to individuals from the United Kingdom? Analyses: To calculate the benefit of averaging, we will subtract the error (MSE) of the average of two estimates from the error of the first estimate (rendering a difference score). The higher this number, the higher the benefit of averaging the first and second estimate (as compared to the accuracy of the first estimate). We will compare this score between the two conditions. For all the tests, we will use mixed-effect models with participants and questions treated as random factors. In addition, we will also log the time it took participants to answer each of the 6 questions. We will compare the time taken to answer each question across conditions to verify whether there is any difference. We will attempt to estimate the likelihood of a null (or alternative, i.e., there is a difference) hypothesis using bayesian statistics. Outliers and exclusions: We will exclude participants that fail an attention check presented at the end of the study. Participants will have to read the full instructions of the attention question and check a specific option. We will also exclude participants that report “yes” to having looked up an answer to any of the questions. Sample size: We will aim to recruit 500 participants per between-subject condition. The sample size will enable us to detect a small effect of Cohen’s d = .20 with 89% power, as calculated by G*Power. This means we plan to collect 1000 participants in total. Stopping rule: We will stop data collection once 1000 participants in total have taken the study on Prolific. Deviations from the planned number of participants are entirely due to the Prolific platform and are outside of our control. Exploratory measures: We do not include any other measures in our study.
