title: Relations between self-regulation, delinquency and psychopathology from adolescence to adulthood
summary: As the data is not yet available to the researchers, unforeseen problems may arise later that will lead to revisions. These revisions and reasons therefore will be communicated openly. 1. Research questions 1) Does self-regulation remain stable from early adolescence to adulthood? 2) To what extent can self-regulation causally predict deviance throughout adolescence and adulthood? 3) To what extent can self-regulation longitudinally predict psychopathology? 4) To what extent are there reciprocal relations between self-regulation and deviance/psychopathology over time? 2. Hypotheses 1) There is medium to high stability of self-regulation over time. There is less stability of self-regulation in vulnerable groups. 2) Low self-regulation predicts deviance over adolescence and adulthood. 3) Low self-regulation predicts psychopathology over adolescence and adulthood. 4) There are reciprocal relations between low self-regulation and deviance/psychopathology over time (i.e., low self-regulation predicts deviance/psychopathology which in turn predicts low self-regulation at the next time point). 3. Data The current study will make use of existing data from a large longitudinal study conducted by CEDAR. The data was not accessible by the researchers at time of registration, coding books were available and one researcher had previously used other parts of this dataset. Researchers looked into the official criminal records in order to assess if these were useful as a measure, but did not conduct any analyses on this data. The sample consists of a group of over 900 participants that were followed from age 10-12 to age 30, during eight measurements. The precise number of participants in the group, and the amount of dropout is presently unknown, making it difficult to specify exact models for analysis. Variables of interest 1) Self-regulation A 92-item dysregulation inventory Mezzich, Tarter, Giancola, & Kirisci (2001) will be used to measure cognitive, emotional and behavioral self-regulation. According to the codebook, this data should be present for all time points. 2) Deviance Deviance will be measured using overlapping items from the CBCL parent/teacher reports (before age 16) and the Youth/Adult self-report (after age 16). Items differ slightly across different measures, but concern the same content. Items seem to reflect major and minor deviance at face value. As double measure (i.e., parent/teacher, teacher/youth) were taken at certain time points, it will be checked if both tap in to the same underlying construct. A confirmatory factor analysis will be done to ensure all items load on a single deviance factor. The items and alternative wordings can be found below. Major deviance items | alternative wordings Destroys property belonging to (his/her family or) others | I (damage or) destroy things belonging to others Gets in many fights | I get in many fights Physically attacks people | I physically attack people Steals | I steal Threatens people | I threaten to hurt people Minor deviance items | alternative wordings Cruelty, bullying or meanness to others | I am mean to others Destroys his/her owns things | I (damage or) destroy my (own) things Doesn’t seem to feel guilty after misbehaving | I don't feel guilty after doing something I shouldn’t Hangs around with other who get in trouble | I hang around with kids/others/people who get in trouble Lying or cheating | I lie or cheat Temper tantrums or hot temper | I have a hot temper Used alcohol or drugs for non-medical purposes | I use alcohol or drugs for non-medical purposes; I use drugs (other than alcohol (and nicotine)) for non-medical purposes Criminal records Criminal records were consulted around 19 years of age, and will be taken in as part of the deviance measure, or as a separate construct, depending on how well these items converge. 3) Psychopathology Psychopathology was measured in a variety of ways at different time points within the data collected by CEDAR. For the current study the aim was to find a general measure of mental health functioning, rather than looking at specific mental disorder diagnoses. There are two measures in the data which might make this possible. First is the Global Assessment of Functioning scores, given by clinicians during diagnostic interviews using the Psychiatric History Marker. Second is the use of symptom counts of the SCID. Both methods have limits, the first due to the possibility of unreliable GAF scores due to the interviews being done by different clinicians. SCID symptom counts on the other hand might show large variation in severity, and when looking at individuals with similar scores, one might have a clinical disorder, where the other might have a collective of minor symptoms scattered over different disorders. 4. Analyses (preliminary) In order to inspect basic stability of self-regulation over time, Spearman’s rank order correlations will be used. Correlation coefficients of the vulnerable and general group will be transformed and compared to each other. A cross-lagged panel design using structural equation modeling will be used to inspect the relations between the different variables over time for the whole group (as the underlying mechanisms should be the same). Two theoretical models will be compared for model fit, one with only effects of self-regulation on crime/psychopathology and one with reciprocal relationships. Changes may be made in an exploratory way in order to improve model fit.

title: The Crowd(s) Within
summary: Research question and hypothesis: The average of two estimates from the same person has been shown to be more accurate than each estimate on its own. Here, we investigate how taking a different perspective when making the second estimate (specifically, the perspective of a friend who often agrees with us, or a friend who often disagrees with us), impacts the benefit of averaging. We expect that the benefit of averaging, calculated by subtracting the mean squared error (MSE) of the average of two estimates, from the MSE of the first estimate, will depend on the type of instructions people get on how to make the second estimate. We expect that averaging the first and second estimate, which was made from the perspective of a friend one often disagrees with, increases the accuracy of the average estimate (as compared to the first estimate). This increase in accuracy of the average estimate is predicted to be larger compared to the condition where, for their second estimate, people are instructed to make a second guess (i.e., same as Vul & Pashler, 2008), or where the second estimate is made from the perspective of a friend one often agrees with. Design: The study will have 3 conditions dependent on the perspective taken in the second estimate: Self vs. Agreeing Friend vs. Disagreeing Friend. In all three between-subject conditions, participants will be instructed to try and answer 6 questions whose answer is always some percentage, ranging from 0% to 100%. The instructions for the second estimate will depend on the condition (see below). In all three conditions, participants will not be told at the beginning that they will have to make a second estimate. Manipulations: In the self perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be told to make a second guess. The same instructions will be used as in Vul and Pasher (2008) and Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, and Vanpaemel (2014). Specifically, the instruction will be: “We will now ask you to provide a second guess at the answer to each of the six questions you were asked in the first session. These answers should not be the same as your previous answers: these should reflect your ‘second guess’.” In the agreeing friend perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be instructed to: “Now picture a friend whose views and opinions are very similar to yours. To illustrate, when discussing politics, you often find yourself agreeing on various issues. How would he or she answer these six questions? Please answer these questions again, but now as this friend.” In the disagreeing friend perspective condition, for the second estimate, participants will be instructed to: “Now picture a friend whose views and opinions are very different from yours. To illustrate, when discussing politics, you often find yourself disagreeing on various issues. How would he or she answer these six questions? Please answer these questions again, but now as this friend.” Dependent variable(s): Participants will be asked to estimate the correct answer of 6 questions whose answer is always a percentage (cf. Vul & Pashler, 2008). They will be able to indicate their answer using a slider that ranges from 0% to 100%. What percent of the world’s airports are in the United States? (answer: 32.3%) What percent of the world’s population lives in China, India, and the European Union? (answer: 43.2%) What percent of the world’s countries have a higher fertility rate than the United States? (answer: 57.7%) What percent of the world’s telephone lines are in China, USA, and the European Union? (answer: 53.3%) Saudi Arabia consumes what percentage of the oil it produces? (answer: 32.5%) What percentage of the world’s countries have a higher life expectancy than the United States? (answer: 19.6%) Participants’ responses will be converted to mean squared errors. Data collection procedure: Data will be collected using the mTurk platform. Participants will be paid a fixed amount for their participation which will be limited to individuals from the United States? Analyses: In order to calculate the benefit of averaging, we will subtract the MSE of the average of two estimates from the MSE of the first estimate (rendering a difference score). The higher this number, the higher the benefit of averaging the first and second estimate (as compared to the accuracy of the first estimate). To test within each respective condition whether the average of the two estimates is more or less accurate than the first estimate (i.e., the within crowd effect), we will use dependent samples t-tests (two-sided). In order to compare the benefit of averaging between the different perspective conditions (i.e., comparing whether the difference score of the MSE of the average and the MSE of the first estimate is different per condition), we will use independent samples t-tests (two-sided). Outliers and exclusions: We will exclude participants that fail an attention check presented at the end of the study. Participants will have to read the full instructions of the attention question and check a specific option. We will also exclude participants that report “yes” to having looked up an answer to any of the questions. Sample size: As our main hypothesis concerns comparing the difference scores of the MSE of the average and the MSE of the first estimate across conditions, we will aim to recruit 450 participants per between-subject condition. The sample size will enable us to detect a small effect of Cohen’s d = .20 with 85% power, and a Cohen’s d = .30 with > 99% power, as calculated by G*Power. This means we plan to collect 1350 participants in total. To counteract exclusions and attention check failures, we will increase the total number of participants to 475 per between-subject condition. Stopping rule: We will stop data collection once 1425 participants in total have taken the study on mTurk. Deviations from the planned number of participants are entirely due to the mTurk platform and are outside of our control. Exploratory measures: We do not include any other measures in our study.

title: Qualitative analysis of measurement reactivity in an experience sampling study
summary: Content: Hypotheses Design Plan Sampling Plan Variables Prior Knowledge of Data Analysis Plan Other Hypotheses This research is exploratory, we have no hypotheses for this analysis. Design Plan Study type Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials. Blinding No blinding is involved in this study. Is there any additional blinding in this study? Participants did not know the intervention group to which they had been assigned. At the beginning of the study, participants did know that there were groups that differ in the amount of time they need to invest and in the incentive they receive (this was stated on the informed consent), but they were not informed about the nature of the other groups. Control questions were included at the end of the study to be able to see to what extent participants were aware of the study hypotheses (see supplementary materials for questions in Dutch). Study design All study procedures have been approved by the Social and Societal Ethics Committee at KU Leuven. A baseline session was followed by a 14 day ESM period. After the ESM period participants returned to the lab for a follow-up session. The individual parts of the study are described in the following paragraphs in more detail. Baseline session After providing informed consent, participants were randomly assigned to one of the six experimental conditions and asked to fill out the baseline questionnaires (previous or current psychopathology, alcohol use, smoking, drug use, demographics & contact information, smartphone use, personality, depression, anxiety, self-esteem, emotion regulation, perceived stress, & momentary and trait affect; all questionnaires that were developed or adapted for this study are provided in the supplementary materials). The six conditions were: a short ESM questionnaire 3 times per day, a short ESM questionnaire 6 times per day, a short ESM questionnaire 9 times per day, a long ESM questionnaire 3 times per day, a long ESM questionnaire 6 times per day, a long ESM questionnaire 9 times per day. The short questionnaire consisted of ± 30 items (depending on branching logic) and the long questionnaire consisted of ± 60 items (depending on branching logic; both questionnaires can be found in the supplementary materials in the original Dutch form and translated to English). Participants were briefed individually about the ESM testing period (the briefing script can be found in the supplementary materials) and practiced filling in the ESM questionnaire to assure that all items were understood by the participants. The briefing lasted approximately 20 minutes. As determined by the randomization procedure, participants were also told how many times per day they would be signaled to complete the questionnaire and how much money they would receive for their participation (the incentive was dependent on the condition; participants in the conditions with 3 beeps per day received 40 euro, while those in the 6 and 9 beep conditions received 60 and 80 euro, respectively). The briefing was conducted in Dutch or English, depending on the researcher conducting the session. 14 Days of ESM The lab visit was followed by the ESM testing period of 14 days. During this time, participants, depending on the experimental condition, received 3, 6, or 9 prompts per day to fill in a short or long questionnaire. Participants had the option to contact the researchers in case of problems. Posttest session After the two weeks of ESM, a second session was conducted during which participants were asked to fill out the posttest questionnaires (burden, social norm & ideal affect, depression, anxiety, self-esteem, emotion regulation, momentary and retrospective affect; all questionnaires that were created or adapted for this study are provided in the supplementary materials). A (randomly chosen) subsample of approximately 10 participants per experimental condition was invited to a qualitative interview lasting approximately 10 minutes, at the end of the posttest session. The qualitative interview was semi-structured, in the sense that participants were asked a series of predetermined questions and follow-up questions were asked depending on the answers (a list of the questions can be found in the supplementary materials). All participants received their compensation and were debriefed about the study after the posttest session. During the debriefing, it was explained that the study consisted of different groups that received different numbers of beeps per day and different questionnaires (see supplementary materials). Participants received 40, 60, or 80 euro in form of gift vouchers depending on the number of beeps per day. The amounts of the incentives were decided during focus groups and based on experiences of researchers with student recruitment at KU Leuven in the past, as well as the available budget. We reduced the incentive to 25, 30, and 40 euro if a participant responded to less than a third of the scheduled beeps during the study (i.e., to less than 14, 28, and 42 beeps in the 3, 6, and 9 beep conditions, respectively). The reduced amount corresponds to the full payment for both lab sessions (20 euro) plus roughly a third of the payment for the ESM period (no exact payments were possible because the payments needed to be made in vouchers of 5 euro). Participants were informed about the existence of a minimum compliance requirement during the briefing, but not about the exact requirement (this sentence was used in the briefing: “If we find that you didn’t fill in enough beeps, you will not get the full payment at the end.”; for the full instructions please see the supplementary materials). Randomization A total of 163 participant were randomly assigned to an experimental condition (see Section sample size for details). Randomization into the different conditions was based on a scheme that ensured that an equal number of participants in each condition started on every day of the week (participants could start on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday). This measure was taken to prevent that time effects would be driven by weekday (e.g., if all participants in one group would start on a Tuesday, a drop of compliance on the 5th ESM day could be purely driven by the fact that the 5th ESM day was always a Saturday; starting a roughly equal number of participants from every condition on every weekday was supposed to assure that these effects cancel out). Ten participants per experimental condition were randomly selected to take part in the qualitative interview. Sampling Plan Existing data Registration following analysis of the data: Part of the data collected during this study have been accessed and analyzed for research questions unrelated to the current investigation, as described under prior knowledge of the data. Specify whether this data is open or publicly available: Data are not publicly available. ESM data collection procedure The ESM period lasted 14 days and was signal contingent. Participants received 3, 6, or 9 beeps, depending on the condition they have been assigned to during the baseline session. Beeps were semi-randomly spread between 9 am and 10:30 pm. In the 3-beep condition, beeps were scheduled randomly in each of three 4 h 30 min windows. In the 6-beep condition, the day was split into six 2 h 15 min windows and a beep was scheduled randomly in each of the windows. In the 9-beep condition, the day was split into 9 1h 30 min windows and one beep scheduled in each of them. There was a no beep window of 20 minutes between consecutive beeps. On day 3, 6, 9, and 12, an instructed response item (i.e., a trick item that was supposed to function as a test if participants were paying attention to the questionnaire) was added to one of the questionnaires. It was always presented at the middle beep in the 3 beep condition and switched between the third and fourth beep in the 6 beep condition. In the 9 beep condition, it was shown once at the fourth beep, once at the sixth beep, and twice at the fifth beep. Due to constraints by the program used, no no-beep window of 20 minutes could be guaranteed between the last beep before the questionnaire with the instructed response item and the questionnaire with instructed response item (i.e., the last beep before the beep with the instructed response item could be less than 20 minutes before the beep with the instructed response item). The same applies to the first questionnaire after the questionnaire with the instructed response item. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a short (~30 items) or long questionnaire (~60 items) during the study. The ESM questionnaires can be found in the supplementary materials. Following a pilot test, we estimated the completion time for the short questionnaire to be around 1,5 min and 2,5 min for the long questionnaire. The phone beeped or vibrated for 90 seconds or until the participant started filling in the questionnaire. After 90 seconds, the questionnaire became unavailable. Once participants started filling in the questionnaire, they had 90 seconds until time out per question (in case of time out, the questionnaire stopped and no subsequent questions were shown). Participants received a phone (motorola DEFY+) with the app mobileQ (Meers et al., 2019) installed on it. Other functions of the phone were fully disabled. At every beep, a start screen of the questionnaire was displayed automatically (see Figure 2). Participants had to press “start survey” on this start screen to proceed to the first question. Sound and vibration could be turned on and off separately by the participants, but they couldn’t be disabled at the same time (if sound was switched off, the vibration was turned on automatically). Notifications did not require an internet connection to be delivered. Sample size (number of participants) Overall study: We aimed to recruit 150 students for the study. Participants were eligible for inclusion if they were Dutch speaking, between 18-30 years old, currently enrolled as a student at a university or hogeschool, and had never taken part in a study that used a phone app before. Participants were recruited via advertisements on Facebook groups for research participants and flyers that were placed on different campuses of KU Leuven and in local bars. Recruitment started on 17.12.18 and testing was conducted between 11.02.19 and 18.07.19. Of the 164 participants that took part in the baseline session, 3 participants had to be excluded because they were not currently enrolled as a student, 2 dropped out during the ESM period, 4 missed more than 1 full day of data because of technical problems (for one participant the battery of the phone broke, for 3 people the time of the phone was reset for unknown reasons which led to beeps not being delivered), for 2 participants the time on the phone was off by more than 1 hour (which lead to the beeps being delivered at wrong times), and 1 participant failed to meet the minimum compliance requirement of one third of the ESM questionnaires started). For all these participants new participants were recruited. The reasoning for this decision was to assure that we would have at least 25 participants per condition in all analyses. Since it was uncertain whether technical problems would appear or participants would complete the study, more participants were included than our original inclusion goal. As soon as it was clear that every group had 25 ‘valid’ cases, no further participants were recruited. Sample used for current analysis: Originally, a subsample of 60 participants (10 per experimental condition) were randomly chosen to take part in a qualitative interview after the end of the ESM period. Some interviews were not conducted due to scheduling problems (e.g., several participants were at the lab at the same time, which made it impossible to conduct a particular interview) or due to exclusion or drop out of participants after randomization. 52 of the planned interviews were conducted. Due to a technical problem during one of the interviews, no recording of this interview is available. Therefore, 51 transcribed interviews are available for analysis. Sample size rationale The overall sample for this study was based on power calculations for a previous analysis of the dataset. Based on practical considerations (i.e. the time needed to conduct and analyze interviews), we chose to interview a subset of 60 participants. This sample was expected to be large enough to obtain a thorough understanding of different experiences of participants during this ESM study. Variables Notes: Only the data used in the current preregistration are described. More information on other data that were collected during this study can be found in the supplementary material and other registrations of the project "The effects of sampling frequency and questionnaire length on perceived burden, compliance, and careless responding in ESM data in a student population". Semi-structured interviews were conducted with a randomly chosen subsample of 52 participants (see sample size for further details). The interviews were conducted in English by Mariam Chichua (master student working on the project), and in Dutch by Tessa Biesemans (research assistant) and G.E.. They were recorded and transcribed (verbatim) by several interns and G.E.. All transcriptions were checked for accuracy by G.E.. At the beginning of the interviews, participants were instructed to talk about their experiences during the ESM study. It was stated that the interview would be based on prepared questions, but participants were encouraged to also report other experiences that were not included in the questions. In an effort to reduce social desirability, it was stressed that there were no right or wrong answers. The semi-structured interviews included the following questions, which were based on the broader literature on ESM: What was it like to fill in the questionnaires in the beginning? What was it like in the end? Do you think you filled the questionnaires in differently depending on whether someone else was around or depending on your location? How? Do you think that filling in the questionnaires had an influence on you? If yes, in what way? Did you learn something about yourself during the study? What do you think about the study? How easy was it to remember how you felt before the beep? Did you ever answer that the beep disturbed you? [If yes] Can you describe in what way you were disturbed? You know that our goal is to better understand people’s daily lives. If you were to set up a smartphone study, what would you do differently? Did you find it difficult at some moments to fill in the questionnaires? Why? Were there moments when you were not able to respond? Can you describe why? Can you explain how you used the following questions during the last week? - It cost effort to answer to the questions - I filled in the questions attentively - Since the last time you filled in a questionnaire were you aware that you missed a beep? (missing data) Why did you not respond? Please select all that applies o I could not respond (on time); o I did not want to respond; o I was too stressed to respond; o I felt burdened by the beep; o Other reason Prior knowledge of data The following analyses of data from this study have been conducted: a. The effects of sampling frequency and questionnaire length on burden, compliance, and careless responding in a student population. https://osf.io/pzx8r/. Compliance and careless responding is known across the different experimental groups. Additionally, information on patterns of missed beeps, temporal increases or decreases in burden over the time of the study, and the use of the objective careless responding item was extracted from the interviews and included in this publication. b. Investigating Careless Responding Detection Techniques in Experience Sampling Methods: https://osf.io/p23yn/?view_only=4ce19176ed51449ab760e4fca3ca6c68. Affect items have been analyzed. c. The effect of ESM on the participants’ emotional awareness: https://osf.io/4p7bf/?view_only=4ce19176ed51449ab760e4fca3ca6c68. No significant changes over time in momentary emotional awareness were detected. Also, sampling frequency did not influence changes in momentary emotional awareness over time. To investigate changes in trait emotional awareness over time, the lack of emotional awareness and the lack of emotional clarity subscales of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale were previously analyzed in two different ways. First, they were merged. The mean of these two scales did not change significantly over time. Subsequently, the lack of emotional awareness and the lack of emotional clarity subscales were analyzed separately. Again, no significant changes over time were detected for the lack of emotional awareness. The lack of emotional clarity was found to increase significantly over time. d. The structure of affect across different experience sampling protocols: https://osf.io/6t5ud. Affect items were analyzed. Five participants had to be excluded from the factor analyses because they showed no variance on at least one of the affect variables. In these analyses, we found that 2365 beeps had missing values on at least one of the affect variables. What prior knowledge do you have at the time of pre-registration about trends in the data set you will be working with? All authors are aware of the previous findings concerning burden, compliance and careless responding and the structure of affect. G.E., P. K and I. M.-G. are aware of the results of the emotional awareness analyses and of the results of “Investigating Careless Responding Detection Techniques in Experience Sampling Methods”. Additionally, G.E. has conducted and transcribed a large part of the qualitative interviews and checked transcriptions of all interviews for accuracy. Analysis Plan Qualitative analysis The semi-structured interviews will be analyzed with thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). A priori, we plan to focus on the following questions - Is the participant referring to reactivity (any emotional, cognitive, or behavioral changes caused by the participation in the study) or not? - Which construct or specific variables are affected? - Are any details on the temporal form of reactivity given? - Is any detail on the type of reactive change given? We will aim to differentiate the following types of change: Alpha change (true change in the construct), beta change (recalibration of measure over time) or gamma change (different construct measured over time; see Golembiewski, Billingsley, & Yeager, 1976) Themes that are not directly related to these questions, but that are identified by the researchers during the analysis of the interviews and considered to be relevant, will be added. The qualitative analysis will involve the following steps: 1. Familiarization with the data: G.E. and an additional researcher will independently read all interviews. 2. Generating initial codes: G.E. and an additional researcher will independently identify relevant parts of the interviews and generate initial codes for each of these parts. Codes will refer to the smallest bits on information that can be identified and that are related to one of the research questions above or to other aspects of measurement reactivity that were not thought of a priori. Codes will be generated in a data-driven manner. 3. Creating themes: The two researchers will each categorize their own codes under overarching themes and if necessary, subthemes. 4. Reviewing themes and subthemes: The two researchers will independently review whether responses classified under the same theme/ subthemes form a coherent group. In case the responses do not form a coherent group, the themes/subthemes will be reconsidered and the new themes/subthemes may be added to accommodate the data better. Next, the researchers will consider all of the themes and subthemes and evaluate if they reflect reports of measurement reactivity in the dataset as a whole accurately. In the case that they do not, the themes and subthemes will be reviewed again. 6. Comparing coding, themes and subthemes and resolving disagreements: The coding and the resulting themes and subthemes identified by the two researchers will be compared and disagreements will be documented and resolved by discussion. The final report will include all themes related to measurement reactivity. Additional themes that are created during the coding, but that are later considered not to be related to measurement reactivity will be reported in the supplemental materials. Other The analysis will be conducted in Nvivo. References: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77-101. NVivo qualitative data analysis software; QSR International Pty Ltd.

title: Social Cognition & Music Study Online
summary: 10/30/19 Social & Clinical Neuroscience Lab (PI, Benjamin A. Tabak) Southern Methodist University Department of Psychology Preregistration for “Social Cognition & Music Study Online” This preregistration describes a new data collection effort that will be used for several purposes. One of the primary objectives is to replicate our initial study examining the association between empathic accuracy (EA) for social stimuli (i.e., targets in a video describing personal experiences; Kern et al., 2013) with EA for music. Previously, undergraduate students at Southern Methodist University completed two EA tasks (i.e., one with social stimuli and one with music stimuli) with either cognitive empathy instructions (e.g., how do you think the target is feeling?) or affective empathy instructions (e.g., how does the target make you feel?). A priori power analysis: In our previous analysis, we found partial correlations between EA for social stimuli and music that averaged r = .25 across the dimensions of discrimination and variance for positive, negative, and total stimuli (for further details on the analysis see Nghiem et al., manuscript under review). Based on these results, a power analysis using G*Power (Faul, Erdfelder, Lang, & Buchner, 2007) determined that at least n = 120 would be needed to detect a main effect at 80% statistical power and 5% Type 1 Error. However, because initial findings tend to inflate effect sizes (Ioannidis, 2008), we set out to nearly double our sample size to n = 200 for each analysis (i.e., cognitive EA for social and music stimuli and affective EA for social and music stimuli). With our target of n = 400, we plan to recruit n = 450-500 online MTurk workers to account for participants who fail our validity checks etc. Participant recruitment: MTurk eligibility requirements include: HIT approval rate: greater than or equal to 90% Location is: United States Number of HITs approved: greater than or equal to 50 HIT visibility: Only Workers who qualify to do my HITs can preview my HITs (e.g., they must meet criteria for HIT approval rate and minimum number of HITs in order to see our HIT). There will be no additional inclusion/exclusion rules beyond living in the US and being over 18 years of age. Measures: The following measures include those that pertain to the study being described in this preregistration, as well as other measures that will be used for unrelated studies. Demographic information including the US state the participant lives in, years of education, age, gender, whether they are a native English speaker, their level of English proficiency, and race/ethnicity. Socioeconomic Status (Barratt, unpublished data) Social Phobia Scale (Mattick & Clarke, 1998) Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (Mattick & Clarke, 1998) Leibowitz Social Anxiety Scale (Liebowitz, 1987) Inventory of Depression & Anxiety Symptoms-II dysphoria & panic subscales (Watson et al, 2012) Big Five Inventory (John & Srivastava, 1999) Autism Spectrum Quotient (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001) Revised Social Anhedonia Scale – short form (Winterstein et al., 2011) Adult Temperament Questionnaire [short form] – Orienting Sensitivity subscale (Evans & Rothbart, 2007) Highly Sensitive Person Scale (Aron & Aron, 1997) Emotional Contagion Scale (Doherty, 1997) Interpersonal Reactivity Index (Davis, 1980) Mood and Anxiety Symptoms Questionnaire – General depression and anhedonic depression subscales (Watson et al., 1995) Toronto Alexithymia Scale (Bagby, Parker, & Taylor, 1994) Political Orientation (unpublished items) Music Empathizing Scale (Kreutz, Schubert, & Mitchell; 2008) Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire – Emotional Evocation subscale (Mas-Herrero et al., 2013) Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index (Müllensiefen et al., 2014) PANAS-X positive, negative, and fatigue subscales (Watson & Clark, 1994) UCLA Loneliness Scale (Russell, Peplau, & Ferguson, 1978; Russell, 1996) Inclusion of Other in the Self Scale – family, close friends, group of friends (Aron, Aron, & Smollan, 1992) Need to Belong Scale (Leary et al., 2013) Social Value Orientation (Murphy, Ackermann, & Handgraaf, 2011) Social Connectedness Scale – Revised (Lee, Draper, & Lee, 2001) Social Provisions Scale (Cutrona & Russell, 1987) Satisfaction with Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985; modified with social life) Satisfaction with Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985) Perceptions of Stressful Interpersonal Events over the past month (modified from Conway et al., 2014) Interpersonal Reactions to Stress (unpublished scale) Procedure: Time commitment for the study will be approximately 1-1.5 hours. Participants are routed from MTurk to a custom website hosted on Google Cloud Platform. Our site was created using Node.js and standard web technologies, and results will be stored in a MySQL database. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups, Cognitive or Affective. They will then complete two computer-based ratings tasks. The procedure consists of two randomized trials: for the Cognitive group, (1) a cognitive "empathic accuracy" task (hereafter, cEA), (2) a cognitive musical empathic accuracy task (cMEA); and for the Affective group, (1) an affective "empathic accuracy task" (aEA), and (2) an affective music empathic accuracy task (aMEA). Empathic accuracy stimuli consist of 8 videos total from Kern et al. (2013). Stimuli are video recordings of individuals describing joyful, sad, and anger-provoking events from their lives. Each video is approximately 2 minutes. While watching, subjects in the Cognitive group provide continuous response evaluations of how negative or positive ("very negative" - "very positive") they believe the person feels using online software. Following each video, subjects respond to a few ratings tasks about each video (e.g., "How much do you identify with the person in this video?"). The procedure for the Affective group is the same, except instead of participants being asked to rate how the person feels, they will be asked how negative or positive they feel (i.e., the participant) while watching each clip. Continuous ratings will be recorded at a sampling rate of 10 Hz, down-sampled to 0.5 Hz. Music EA stimuli consist of 12 music recordings originally created for this experiment to express the target primary emotions of joy/happiness, sadness, anger, and tenderness (these stimuli will not be analyzed in the present study). Recordings are 1-2 minutes. In the Cognitive group, subjects will listen to the excerpts and provide continuous response evaluations of how negative or positive ("very negative"= "very positive") they perceive the music to be using online software. Following each music recording, participants will use the same rating scales, identical to the EA task. The procedure for the Affective group is the same, except instead of participants being asked to rate what they perceive the music to convey, they will be asked how negative or positive they feel (i.e., the participant) while listening to each recording. Questions post videos: cEA Q1: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 9 = Extremely) How SIMILAR do you feel you are to this person? Q2: 9-point scale (1 = Very negative; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how positive or negative do you think the person was feeling? aEA Q1: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 9 = Extremely) How SIMILAR do you feel you are to this person? Q2: 9-point scale (1 = Very negative; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how did you feel while watching this video? Questions post music stimuli: cMEA Q1: 9-point scale (1 = Strongly dislike; 5 = Neutral; 9 = Strongly like) How much did you like that music? Q2: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 5 = No opinion; 9 = Very much) Overall, do you relate to this music? Q3: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 5 = No opinion; 9 = Very much) Overall, how ACCURATE do you think you were about your perceptions of what the musician was trying to express in this performance? Q4: 9-point scale (1 = Very negative; 5 = Neither negative nor positive; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how POSITIVE or NEGATIVE do you think the musician meant this performance to be? Q5: scale (1 = Very negative; 5 = Neither negative nor positive; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how positive or negative do you feel the MUSICIAN FELT when creating this music? aMEA Q1: 9-point scale (1 = Strongly dislike; 5 = Neutral; 9 = Strongly like) How much did you like that music? Q2: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 5 = No opinion; 9 = Very much) Overall, do you relate to this music? Q3: 9-point scale (1 = Not at all; 5 = No opinion; 9 = Very much) Overall, did you feel that your emotional reactions to this piece correspond to what the musician intended to express? Q4: 9-point scale (1 = Very negative; 5 = Neither negative nor positive; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how POSITIVE or NEGATIVE do you feel the musician meant this performance to be? Q5: scale (1 = Very negative; 5 = Neither negative nor positive; 9 = Very positive) Overall, how positive or negative do you feel the MUSICIAN FELT when creating this music? Statistical Analysis We will use a novel Bayesian hierarchical modeling method (Nghiem et al., manuscript under review) to calculate bias, discrimination, and variance estimates from participant time series data, then correlate these estimates across social and music conditions. We will also examine the relationship between our primary variables of interest using standard time series correlation methods for analysis of EA (e.g., Zaki, Bolger & Ochsner, 2008), in which participants’ lag-1 time series are Fisher r-to-z transformed then compared across conditions (video and music). Covariation associated with musical training of participants and emotional expressivity of videos will be modeled using partial correlation. Exploratory analyses will also consider the extent to which relevant moderators improve performance across social and music EA. These moderators include the Autism Quotient (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001), the perspective taking (IRI-PT) and/or empathic concern (IRI-EC) subscales of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; Davis, 1980), and potentially, other relevant moderators. In our initial lab data, we calculated linear mixed effects models to test for a possible moderating role of these individual differences on EA for video/music in positive/negative valence conditions. Two versions of the models were run on both affective and cognitive groups: (1) with time-series correlation coefficients as the outcome, and (2) with the Bayesian discrimination parameter as the outcome. Participants were modelled as random effects. Wald chi-squared tests were calculated from mixed models using the car package in R (Fox & Weisberg, 2010). For the time-series correlation version of the analysis, in the affective group IRI-PT showed a borderline significant interaction with stimulus valence (p = .047); all other main fixed effects and interactions involving individual differences—including the cognitive group—were not significant. However, analysis of the discrimination parameter revealed a main fixed effect of IRI-EC on EA in the affective group (p = .002). No other evidence of moderation was found.

title: Behavioural Consistency in Smartphone Use
summary: Behavioural Consistency in Application Use Background: The proposed research aims to assess whether digital traces of behaviour, specifically smartphone use, show within-person consistency across time and context. Time in this project is defined as different days of the week, and context is defined as the specific application a person is using. Using pre-existing data sets, which collected smartphone use from the same person over several days, it is possible to assess if application usage time, and application number of pickups is consistent across apps (context) and across days (time). We will mirror work conducted by Shoda, Mischel, & Wright, (1994) which outlines how to create intraindividual situation-behaviour profiles and further assess the similarity in the ‘shapes’ of these profiles across days of data from each person. Data: We have obtained app usage data from several datasets. This included the LiveLab dataset, (Shepard, Rahmati, Tossell, Zhong, & Kortum, 2011), the Consumer Mobile Experience dataset (OFCOM, 2019), the Securacy dataset (Jones, Ferreira, Hosio, Goncalves, & Kostakos, 2015), the Mobile Phone Usage (MPU) dataset (Pielot et al., 2017), Health and Smartphone Use dataset (Shaw, Ellis, Geyer, Ziegler, & Davidson, 2018), the Tsinghu App datset (Yu, Li, Xu, Zhang, & Kostakos, 2018), the CARAT dataset (Oliner, Iyer, Stoica, Lagerspetz, & Tarkoma, 2013), the Student Life dataset (Wang et al., 2014) and the Mobile Data Challenge (MDC) dataset (Kiukkonen, Blom, Dousse, Gatica-perez, & Laurila, 2010). We established some inclusion criteria to assess suitability of these datasets. Specifically, datasets had to contain time stamps of foreground application use so we could examine what application was on screen (a person’s context) at each time, and for how long. Consequently, four of these datasets were unsuitable for our analysis. The Tsinghu App dataset only included app categories and not the specific applications used. The CARAT dataset had data whereby lots of applications were documented as being used at the same time, including multiple simultaneous foreground applications. Therefore, it was difficult to establish which application was on the screen and being used at each time stamp. The Student Life dataset only recorded running applications and not foreground application use. Finally, it was only possible in the Mobile Data Challenge (MDC) dataset to determine when a new app appeared in the foreground, but not when the use of that particular app ended due to a lack of screen state data. The remaining datasets required standardisation so they could be combined and analysed as a single dataset. All datasets were converted to this format, with these column headers: PersonID, DataSet, Application, Start_Time_Stamp, End_Time_Stamp, Duration_Sec, Age, Gender. Each row represented a single app use event. The steps to do this standardisation included: Stage 1: 1. Unix timestamps were converted to ‘human readable’ timestamps which represented the local time (rather than universal time) for each participant. 2. Within the datasets which had Age data; Age was converted from an interval variable to a categorical variable with these categories: 18-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55+. This was to match data from the Consumer Mobile Experience dataset which contained age data to this categorical resolution. 3. Character data specifying gender was converted to either “MALE” or “FEMALE’. 4. Durations of each app event were calculated if this was not already a variable in the dataset. 5. Duration data was converted to seconds and rounded to two decimal places. 6. If not present in the original dataset, End_Time_Stamp was calculated as follow: Start_Time_Stamp + Duration_Sec. 7. Data was ordered by Person ID and Start_Time_Stamp. Stage 2 – For the 100 most used applications: 1. Chrome and Browser were re-categorised as ‘Internet’ to establish uniformity no matter what browser application was native to each type of smartphone. 2. Package names e.g. “com.facebook.katana’ were converted to human readable names e.g. “Facebook”. 3. Different brands had different package names for their native clock app. All were converted to “Clock”. 4. Removed data from people who had less than 9 days of data and less than 9 app events. This left 824 people in the sample. 5. For each person, removed data from the first and last day of their data. This insured only full days were measured. 6. Removed any events that had a duration that was a negative number. 7. For the final combined dataset, only included applications that were used by over 25% of the same (>206 people) and applications which were not system apps. Analysis to pre-register: Following processing, we have a final dataset of 820 people with longitudinal (>7 days) application data. Following the procedure of Shoda, Mischel, & Wright, (1994), it is possible to create daily behaviour profiles of application use. The consistency of these daily behaviour profiles can be assessed within the same person by comparing their behaviour profiles across the many days of data we have for that person. Daily behaviour profiles can be created for 2 types of smartphone behaviours; daily app time, and daily app number of pickups. This requires the generation of 2 new datasets for each participant: Daily App Time Dataset 1. Isolate data from X participant. 2. Remove days of data where none of the 21 apps were used. 3. Calculate for each app the daily total usage time in seconds across all days of data that we have for that person. 4. Ensure that this daily calculation accounts for switching to and from Daylight saving time. The start and ends of each day will be adjusted accordingly. Daily App Pickups Dataset 1. Isolate data from X participant. 2. Remove days of data where none of the 21 apps were used. 3. Calculate for each app the daily total number of pickups (as a count/frequency) across all days of data that we have for that person. 4. Ensure that this daily calculation accounts for switching to and from Daylight saving time. The start and ends of each day will be adjusted accordingly. Independently for each smartphone behaviour, behaviour profiles for each person will be created as follows: 1. Place everyone’s daily usage data together into one dataset column wise. This means that each row in the dataset will represent one of the 21 apps, and each column will represent a person and a day of their data (e.g. Person 1, Day 1). 2. A normative profile of daily application usage for the 21 apps will be calculated by averaging each row. 3. Standard deviations will also be calculated for each row. Then, to make a behaviour profile for a particular person and day: 1. Extract data from person X, day X. 2. Subtract the normative profile from person X, day X. 3. Then scale this by dividing these new values by the standard deviations for each app (see above) that were calculated from everyone’s data. Behaviour profiles per day can be compared within participants by conducting ipsative correlations (see Shoda et al., 1994). Scaled values from the 21 apps from person X day X can be compared to scaled values from person X day Y using correlations. However, prior to conducting the correlations, the scaled daily usage values per app will be converted to ranks (Lowest used app = 1, Highest used app = 21). Higher consistency in the ranks across days would equate to higher coefficients. Therefore, the correlation coefficient essentially reflects the stability of the rank order among the interpersonal situations (apps) within the same individual and furthermore how an individual’s usage in each situation (app) deviates from the respective normative usage of each app. It is predicted that: Hypothesis 1: Within-person smartphone use across days will be statistically and significantly higher than between-person smartphone use across days. Hypothesis 2: There will be consistency in smartphone usage across weekdays and weekends, resulting in an ipsative correlation co-efficient of .8 or higher. Confirmatory Analysis – Inferential Statistics: 1. We will test consistency using two kinds of behavioural profiles: day pairs and split halves. Day pairs will involve a selection of two random daily use profiles from the data set, on which an ipsative correlation is calculated. Split halves will involve the same comparison but calculated on an average of 50% of the individual’s daily profiles. That is, we will average the use profile over half of the individual’s data where the days averaged are selected randomly. This 50% profile will then be compared to another 50% profile (of either the same user or different user) using an ipsative correlation. We use the Split halves both because of the potential for high variation in daily usage and because some users will have more day profiles than others, and therefore have a greater influence on the day pairs analysis. 2. The ipsative correlations derived from the Day Pair and Split Halve comparisons will provide the data for permutation tests. Specifically, for the Day pairs, we will compare the distribution of correlations from between-subject pairs with the distribution of correlations from within-subject pairs (i.e., compare random pairs to pairs associated with the same user). For the Split halves, we will undertake the same comparison but use the Split half average data. We will run ~3,000,000 comparisons, which will provide approximately 10 samplings of each potential permutation (using the formula n(n-1))/2 to determine the exact amount). Exploratory analysis 1. To visualise if…then… patterns of behaviour for each person, conditional inference decision trees will be conducted with application name as the criterion variable and the daily usage statistic (either daily pickups or daily usage time) for each app as the independent variable. Data used to train the tree can either be from one person (intraindividual situation-behaviour profile), or from all people (normative profile).

title: Childhood Obesity and Stigma toward Parents
summary: In Study 1, we asked: (1) Do social perceivers stigmatize parents of children (here, daughters) with obesity more than parents of average/healthy-weight children? (We expect this.) (2) Does stigma transfer from obese children to average-weight parents (as a stigma-by-association account might predict)? (We did not expect this, but we found some support for it.) (3) Does parent gender moderate stigma toward parents of obese children, such that mothers are more stigmatized? (We predicted this and found some support.) (4) Might this be driven by perceptions that mothers (vs. fathers) are relatively more responsible for offspring appearance/weight? (We explored this and found instead that perceptions that parents of children with obesity [vs. average/healthy-weight] possess negative parenting qualities drove stigmatization.) In Study 2, we aim to replicate those findings and extend this to exploring sons as well as daughters.

title: neural correlats of feeling generation-LRP&nond
summary: The aim of this document is to specify the analysis described briefly in https://osf.io/z8xqp regarding the LRP component of the ERP data and the non-decision (nond) parameter of the Linear Ballistic Accumulator (LBA) model. It will be performed on previously collected data. The Lateralized Readiness Potential (LRP) is an ERP component indicating motor planning. In other words, it is present once the participant has made a decision and is getting ready to execute its related motor action (e.g., keypress). According to the LBA model, the nond parameter represents the sum of all non-decision processes (e.g. early perceptual processes, motor planning). Thus, it is logical to predict that (a) the LRP and nond will be positively correlated and that (b) the duration of motor programming, as assessed using the response-locked LRP will be shorter than nond. All analysis will be performed on both the emotional task, and the faces (cognitive) task. Hypothesis We hypothesize that the duration of the response-locked LRP-onset (i.e. the time window between the onset of the LRP and the response itself) will be shorter than the estimated nond, with the difference representing the duration of early perceptual processes. Moreover, we hypothesize that there will be a negative correlation between the response-locked LRP duration (as estimated using the LOTO methodology; Gluth & Meiran, 2019) and the nond. LOTO estimates are reverse, such the longer LRP duration obtained by the LOTO, represent a participant with faster LRP duration than the group. Practically, we hypothesize that longer LRP durations will be associated with smaller nond estimates. Data cleaning and analysis We will exclude from all analysis (both modeling and EEG) trials with response time (RT) shorter than 200 ms. There are no deviant participants (participants with low percent of normative responses in the emotional task or low accuracy rate in the faces task). We will exclude deviant stimuli from the emotional task. Stimuli will be excluded if the proportion of normative response is below .55. This proportion will be calculated using the data from the current as well as from previous experiment conducted on different participants (with the same methodology, but with no EEG data recorded). Stimuli excluded will be also excluded from the LRP analysis. Nond Per-subject nond will be estimated using hierarchical modeling, specifically by using the 'ggdmc' package in r. Priors will be the same priors as those used successfully in modeling this task in other experiments in the lab. Specifically: pop.mean<-c(2,2,.3,2,.5) names(pop.mean)<-GetPNames(model) pop.scale<-c(.6,.6,.1,.8,.8) names(pop.scale)<-GetPNames(model) prior.beta <- c(rep(1,npar)) names(prior.beta)<-GetPNames(model) #prior p.prior<-BuildPrior( dists = rep("tnorm", npar), p1 = pop.mean, p2 = pop.scale, lower = c(rep(0,npar)), upper = pop.mean+pop.scale*8) mu.prior <- BuildPrior( dists = rep("tnorm", npar), p1 = pop.mean, p2 = pop.scale, lower = c(rep(0,npar)), upper = pop.mean+pop.scale*8) sig<-c(rep(1,npar)) names(sig)<-GetPNames(model) sigma.prior<- BuildPrior( dists = rep("beta", npar), p1 = sig, p2 = sig, lower = c(rep(0,npar)), upper = c(rep(3,npar))) LRP Data will be analyzed using a combination of routines from the EEGLAB MATLAB© toolbox (Delorme & Makeig, 2004) and custom code. Data will first be down-sampled to 250 Hz and high-pass filtered (cut-off 1Hz). Subsequently, a customized adaptive filter will be applied to suppress line-noise. This will be followed by Artifact Subspace Reconstruction (Mullen et al., 2015), re-referencing to the mean and low-pass filtering (cutoff 40Hz). Next, Infomax ICA was applied(Bell & Sejnowski, 1995). The resulting independent components (ICs) will be evaluated automatically for artifacts, by combining spatial, spectral, and temporal analysis of ICs. ICs identified as containing ocular, muscular, or cardiac artifacts will be removed from data. Based on "Detecting the onset of the lateralized readiness potential: A comparison of available methods and procedures" (Mordkoff & Gianaros, 2000), we will asses response locked LRP onset using a regression based method (their 1DF model), were we will fit 2 separate regression lines to each participant's LRP wave-form. One for the pre-onset period (constant at zero) and another for the post-onset period (a straight line connecting zero at the LRP-onset time point and peak LRP amplitude) the (single) parameter of this model is LRP-onset. As recommended by Mordkoff and Gianaros, we will use the Jackknife method to assess the SD across participants. We will use LOTO (Gluth & Meiran, 2019) to assess the rank-ordering of individuals in terms of their LRP-onset. We will then estimate the positive Pearson correlation between the LOTO estimates of LRP-onset and the ‘ggdmc’ estimates of individual nond. We will use a single t-test (Bayesian) to assess the difference between the mean ggdmc estimated nond and the average LRP-onset Bell, A. J., & Sejnowski, T. J. (1995). title: Science beliefs, political ideology, and cognitive sophistication
summary: A formatted word document of this preregistration is attached. The purpose of this study is to examine the extent to which people believe specific science topics and science facts (used in Studies 1 and 2) are politically divisive. Information from this study will be used to evaluate and reorganize the results that are already reported in Studies 1 and 2. The original goal of this set of studies was to generate a fairly comprehensive set of scientific issues in order to test several theoretically derived predictions. These predictions concerns tests of motivated reasoning and the politicization of science beliefs, but they also concern the extent to which science knowledge is a predictor of a range of science beliefs. Thus, political disagreement is not relevant to every analysis in this set of studies. Therefore, we outline a set of procedures below determining how we will use the information obtained in this test. Participants Participants (N = 200) are recruited from Lucid. Method Subjects are asked to consider 17 statements (e.g. "Global warming is at least partly caused by human activity and is a serious problem for the environment.") and 12 science facts (e.g. "Electrons are smaller than atoms") and are asked: "Do you think this is something that Democrats and Republicans are likely to disagree on?" Options are Yes or No. All items are presented in randomized order. Analysis All items are analyzed individually: The percentage of 'Yes' responses (e.g. indicating the belief that Democrats and Republicans would disagree) for each statement is calculated. The percentage of 'Yes' responses for each science fact is also calculated. Analysis script is attached. Data will be interpreted in percentages, only. There is no exclusion criteria; missing data will be treated as follows: If a subject is missing data on an item, they will be excluded from that calculation but will be included in other analyses for which they have data. Results Science statements with 50% agreement or greater will be considered politically divisive for the purposes of this study. We choose a 50% cutoff so that we can include a range of items that are politically divisive to a greater and lesser extent. That is, we don't want a set of only highly divisive items, but we want to identify meaningful disagreement. However, we do want to remove items for which there is unlikely to be any level of political disagreement (i.e. where agreement is less than 50%) from relevant analyses. No non-divisive items will be removed from analyses comparing the predictive power of ideology and deficit models. This includes tests of Fisher's r-to-z, and regression analyses using the composite liberal and conservative pro-science scales. Non-divisive items will be identified in all analyses using individual items, but the analyses as currently reported will remain the same. This includes the individual items correlations and the tests of political X cognitive sophistication interactions for each individual item. The 12 science facts are included here for comparative purposes only; we will not change any analyses or calculations based on whether or not people think these items are divisive.

Then standardize the regression coefficients using Fisher’s transformation (i.e., Fisher-transformed within-person by-attribute slopes) 2. SP for intelligence is calculated as the mean of participants’ SP for: “intelligent,” “smart,” and “intellectually sharp.” SP for confidence is calculated as the mean of participants’ SP for: “confident,” “self-assured,” and “charismatic.” a. If the inclusion of an item results in a drop of .01 or more in Cronbach’s alpha of the SP for either intelligence or confidence, then that item would be dropped from the calculations. 3. The simple correlations (rs) in the table above will be calculated by regressing a given predictor (SP/FP for intelligence/confidence) on a DV (e.g., interest [in a single website]), then obtaining the standardized regression coefficient. For choice variables, logit regression coefficients will be obtained, then transformed to r via log odds ratio. 4. The partial correlations in SEM (rpSEM) in the table above will be calculated by conducting a structural equation model in which the SPs for intelligence and for confidence (or the FPs for intelligence and for confidence) are modelled as latent factors and then simultaneously regressed on the DV. Latent factor SP for a given attribute will be indicated by SP for the corresponding three items (intelligence: “intelligent,” “smart,” and “intellectually sharp”; confidence: “confident,” “self-assured,” and “charismatic”). Latent factor FP for a given attribute will be indicated by four parcel-level FP for that attribute. Parcel-level FP will be calculated by randomly dividing the 100 targets into four parcels (25 targets each) and following the FP calculation procedure above (#1). The rpSEM for SP (or FP) on a given attribute is the standardized path coefficient of that SP (or FP) after controlling for the SP (or FP) for the other attribute. 5. The partial correlations (rp) in the table above will be calculated by regressing the SPs for intelligence and for confidence (or the FPs for intelligence and for confidence) simultaneously on a DV, then obtaining the standardized partial regression coefficient of a SP (or FP), controlling for the other SP (or FP).
